COMPASS: A Comparative Evaluation of Transformer-Based Abstractive Summarization Models with Composite Semantic Scoring on CNN/DailyMail Dr. A. Maheshwari Associate Professor Department of Computational Intelligence SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Kattankullathur Chennai, India maheshwa1@srmist.edu.in Abel Kurian Sangeeth Undergraduate Student Department of Computational Intelligence SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Kattankullathur Chennai, India as8259@srmist.edu.in Sanish Joseph Undergraduate Student Department of Computational Intelligence SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Kattankullathur Chennai, India sj6879@srmist.edu.in Abstract—Text summarization is an important task in the face of the steadily increasing amount of online news. This paper introduces COMPASS (Comparative Multi-model Pipeline with Adaptive Semantic Scoring), a multi-model summarization system which evaluates five transformer models, T5-Base, T5Large, BART-large-CNN, PEGASUS-large, mT5-multilingual in a single pipeline that can process inputs supporting diverse input types like text, PDFs, and URLs. We use the CNN/Daily Mail dataset to evaluate all with ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L, BLEU, METEOR and BERTScore F1, and a weighted composite of composite scoring technique that favours semantic quality over lexical overlap. Our results show that BART- large-CNN has the best results on all metrics, recording ROUGE-1 (0.445), BERTScore F1 (0.870), and a composite score of 0.4268, followed by PEGASUS (0.4215). BERTScore F1, which has the largest weight of 25% in scoring scheme, is the most discriminative scoring metric, as it measures semantic matching beyond simple level n-gram overlap. mT5-multilingual has the lowest scores due to its multilingual generalisation goal rather than newsdomain specialization. The study also demonstrates the balance between quality and efficiency across model sizes, and introduces a dynamic model selection approach that considers input length, format and language. COMPASS offers a scalable, evaluationrich platform for multi-domain automatic summarization research. Our results show that BART- large-CNN has the best results on all metrics, recording ROUGE-1 (0.445), BERTScore F1 (0.870), and a composite score of 0.4268, followed by PEGASUS (0.4215). Although fast and simple, they were unable to produce capturing the rich contextual and semantic features in text, hence restricting the quality, smoothness and coherence of the ated summaries. Their surface lexical features meant that structurally important sentences could be
 missed when the meaning was conveyed through different words or complex syntactic constructions. The development of neural networks brought abstractive summarization using sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) mod- els using Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. Ferreira et al. [2] presented a contextual text summarizer that included discourse and context in the scoring of scoring, with enhanced context awareness compared purely statistical approaches. Dhanda and Gupta [3] also condressed this by suggesting a new machine learning-based based approach to summarization, moving away from feature engineering to learned representations of text. sentations. These neural models showed a better ability to produce human summaries. However, they had inherent problems such as vanishing graients, fixed length context windows, and severely degraded performance on longer documents. The lack of efficiency of recurrent architectures to efficiently model long range dependencies neck for sequences of arbitrary length. neck, especially in news articles and reports where key information is spread throughout the text. The game-changer in Natural Language Processing has been the advent of the Transformer model, which uses self-attention to capture long depencies over the entire input sequence at once, rather taneously rather than in a sequential manner. This allowed for pretraining on large datasets and greatly significantly boosted performance on a wide range of NLP tasks such as summarization. Gupta et al. [4] detail how to use NLP pipelines based on transformers for summarization, showing improvements in coherence and earlier recurrent approaches. Kumar et els [5]also demonstrate the success of transformer modal in different types of documents and diverse domains, confirming their potential for practical use in summarization tasks. The ability of transformers to consider all input a sequence at once, simultaneously considering local and global contextual relationships, offered a significant RNN-based systems.However, most studies in this era tested a single transformer model, providing little comparative understanding of the relative merits and trade offs of various architectures for the same summarization task. A number of transformers have since achieved state-of-theart results on summarization tasks. BART, a model with a bidirectional encoder and autoregressive decoder is especially adept at abstractive summarization of narrative and newscvlike text because of pretraining on document reconstruction tasks. But most of these systems only evaluate a single model with a single input format, and their evaluation is primarily based on lexical metrics like ROUGE and BLEU, which are known to known to penalise valid paraphrases and synonyms - a a major problem for getting at the semantic adequacy of generated summaries. Comparative studies have started to address the need for multiple models, but there is still much to be done. Muia et al. [15] compare transformer-based models for transformers for summarizing news articles, conducting different models on common datasets and discuss the dilemmas between lexical and semantic fluency in generated outputs. Bani-Almarjeh and Kurdy [9] extend the Arabic abstractive summarization from a comparative perspective with both RNN and transformer models, showing that the benefits of transformer models extend to erate to other languages and scripts. El-Kassas et al. [10]pro- give a survey of automatic text summarization methods including statistical, neural and transformer-based methods, providing a wide-ranging overview of the evolution and ongoing evaluation problems. While these compara- tive studies offer important baselines, but are confined to to lexicalbased evaluation metrics and single domain datasets, and so confine their insights to a narrow range of real-world summarisation tasks. The awareness of the need for semantic evaluation has essential supplement to lexical measures has influenced recent research directions. Adhikari [11] reviews NLP-based machine based approaches to summarisation, pointing out the in- sufficiency of n-gram overlap measures for paraphrase quality and meaning. Gambhir and Gupta [12]pro- give an overview of recent work in automatic text summarization techniques, calling for more sophisticated evaluation beyond simple word matching. Pan et al. [13] present a sequence-tosequence summarization model that that uses a topic-based attention model, and show that attention-based models can produce more topically coherent summaries. Gupta et al. [14] also explore transformer-based systems for automated news summariza- systems, highlighting the need for assessment methods that assess lexical and semantic faithfulness. The use of embedding scores like BERTScore, which measures semantic similarity based on token embeddings as a key improvement to overcome these limitations. has been a major step towards resolving these issues. Despite this, no previous work has comprehensively combined lexical and semantic metrics into a single, weighted composite assessment scheme across various transformer models, and a variety of different inputs input formats simultaneously. The current research literature, although abundant in approaches ranging from statistical methods [1], [5], neural sequence models [2], [3], and transformer-based architectures [4], [6]–[8], reveals a consistent structural gap: systems are predominantly evaluated in isolation, on single input formats, and against narrow lexical metric sets. Comparative studies [9], [10], [15] and evaluation surveys [11], [12] confirm the need for unified benchmarking frameworks that incorporate semantic assessment alongside traditional lexical measures. COMPASS addresses this divide by unifying five transformer-based abstractive models — T5-Base, T5-Large, BART-large-CNN, PEGASUS-large, and mT5-multilingual — within a single comparative pipeline, and by introducing a weighted composite scoring mechanism that integrates ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L, BLEU, METEOR, and BERTScore F1 for holistic, semantically grounded
 model evaluation across heterogeneous input formats including plain text, PDF files, and web URLs. III. DATASET DESCRIPTION The CNN/DailyMail dataset is one of the most widely used benchmarks for automatic text summarization. It consists of news articles collected from CNN and Daily Mail, each paired with human-written summaries known as ”highlights.” These highlights serve as gold-standard reference summaries for evaluating the quality of machine-generated outputs. The large scale and high annotation quality of the dataset make it well-suited for both training and benchmarking extractive and abstractive summarization models. The dataset contains approximately 287,113 training samples, 13,368 validation samples, and 11,490 test samples. Each sample consists of a full-length news article as the source text paired with a journalist-written summary comprising several sentences. The average article length is approximately 781 tokens, while the average summary length is 56 tokens. This substantial compression ratio makes the dataset particularly appropriate for evaluating the contextual understanding and information distillation capacity of summarization models. In this study, the dataset is accessed through the HuggingFace Datasets library, which provides standardized and preprocessed splits. Model-specific tokenizers corresponding to each transformer architecture — T5, BART, PEGASUS, and mT5 — are applied during preprocessing. Input sequences are truncated to a maximum of 1,024 tokens to satisfy transformer input constraints, and summary sequences are capped at 128 tokens. Padding is applied where necessary to ensure batch consistency during training. CNN/DailyMail is particularly well-suited for context-sensitive summarization tasks, as news articles are structured narratives involving multiple named entities, temporal sequences, and causal relationships. This structural richness challenges transformer-based models to capture long-range dependencies and semantic coherence across the full document. As all five models in COMPASS are evaluated on this same dataset under identical experimental conditions, it provides a reliable, consistent, and fair basis for comparative analysis. IV. PROPOSED SYSTEM / ARCHITECTURE Architecture Diagram Fig. 1. Architecture of the proposed COMPASS framework for multi-model text summarization. COMPASS is a multi-model transformer-based text summarization system designed to handle heterogeneous input formats and evaluate multiple summarization architectures under a unified framework. The system architecture is modular and consists of five core components: 1) Input Ingestion and Routing Module — Detects the format of the submitted input (plain text, PDF, or URL) and routes it to the appropriate preprocessing pipeline. 2) Dataset Management Module — Manages dataset loading, preprocessing, and split management using the HuggingFace Datasets library, with model-specific tokenization applied per architecture. 3) Model Training and Summarization Pipeline — Hosts five transformer-based abstractive models: T5-Base, T5Large, BART-large-CNN, PEGASUS-large, and mT5multilingual, each fine-tuned on CNN/DailyMail under identical hyperparameter configurations. 4) Evaluation Engine — Computes ROUGE-1, ROUGE2, ROUGE-L, BLEU, METEOR, and BERTScore F1, and aggregates them into a weighted composite score for holistic model ranking. 5) User Interface (Streamlit-based) — Provides an interactive interface for input submission, model selection, summary generation, metric visualization, and result comparison. The system workflow proceeds as follows. The user submits input through the interface, which is detected and routed by the ingestion module. The input is then preprocessed using the model-specific tokenizer, with sequences truncated to 1,024 tokens and summaries capped at 128 tokens. The preprocessed input is passed to the selected transformer model, which generates the summary. The evaluation engine then scores the output across all metrics and computes the composite rank. Final summaries and evaluation results are presented to the user through the Streamlit interface. A. Input Ingestion and Routing The system supports plain text, PDF files, and URLs as input formats. The routing module automatically detects the input type and directs it to the appropriate preprocessing pipeline. For PDF inputs, text is extracted prior to tokenization. For URLs, the article body is retrieved and cleaned before processing. Language detection is additionally performed to route non-English inputs to the mT5-multilingual model. B. Abstractive Summarization with Transformer Models The abstractive summarization pipeline incorporates five encoder-decoder transformer models: T5-Base, T5-Large, BART-large-CNN, PEGASUS-large, and mT5-multilingual. Each model is fine-tuned on the CNN/DailyMail dataset using a consistent hyperparameter configuration to ensure fair and reproducible comparison. Models are trained for 3 epochs with a batch size of 8, a learning rate of 2×10−5, and the AdamW optimizer with a linear decay scheduler. The maximum input length is set to 1,024 tokens and the maximum summary length to 128 tokens.
 C. Dynamic Model Selection COMPASS incorporates a dynamic model selection mechanism that adapts to the characteristics of the input. Input length, language, and format are used as selection signals: PEGASUS is prioritized for longer news-style documents, while mT5-multilingual is applied for non-English inputs. This selection strategy improves summarization efficiency by matching input properties to the most suitable architecture. D. Evaluation Engine COMPASS includes a comprehensive evaluation module that assesses summary quality across multiple dimensions. Standard lexical metrics — ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGEL, BLEU, and METEOR — measure n-gram overlap between generated and reference summaries. BERTScore F1 provides semantic evaluation by computing similarity using contextual token embeddings. Custom measures, including the abstractiveness score and compression ratio, assess paraphrasing capability and information density respectively. A weighted composite scoring mechanism aggregates all metrics into a single performance score using the following weights: ROUGE-1 (0.20), ROUGE-2 (0.20), ROUGEL (0.15), BLEU (0.10), METEOR (0.10), and BERTScore F1 (0.25). This composite score enables consistent, holistic ranking of all evaluated models. E. User Interface The user interface is implemented using Streamlit, providing an interactive platform for end-to-end summarization. Users can submit input in supported formats, select a summarization model, generate summaries, and view evaluation metrics. Additional features include result comparison across models, copy-to-clipboard functionality, session history tracking, and graphical visualization of metric scores. V. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS Evaluation Metrics Across All Models Fig. 2. Evaluation Metrics Across All Models Fig. 2 shows how each model performed on six evaluation metrics. The n-gram overlap measures (ROUGE-1, ROUGE2, ROUGE-L, BLEU, METEOR) produce scores between 0.06 and 0.45, which are sensitive to word-to-word matches between the generated and reference summaries. Conversely, BERTScore F1 — calculated using the contextual token embeddings of BERT — has a consistent score of 0.83–0.87 across all models. This reflects a general limitation of ngram metrics, which penalize valid paraphrases and synonyms. BERTScore balances this by assessing semantic rather than surface similarity. BART-CNN achieves the best BERTScore F1 (0.870), closely followed by PEGASUS (0.867), proving that architecturally more powerful models also generate semantically richer summaries. Radar Chart: Per-Model Metric Profile Fig. 3. Comparison of Accuracy Across Models Fig. 3 provides radar charts for each of the five models and gives a holistic view of the strength distribution across all metrics simultaneously. The BERT-F1 axis protrudes much further than the ROUGE/BLEU/METEOR axes in all models, validating that semantic quality consistently exceeds surfacelevel n-gram overlap. BART-CNN and PEGASUS demonstrate the largest and most balanced polygon areas, indicating competence across a broad range of n-gram and semantic metrics. mT5-Multi has the smallest total area, as it is trained for multilingual generalization rather than specialization on English news summarization. This visualization shows that higher-BERTScore models are also more likely to have higher n-gram scores, albeit not proportionately — semantic quality can improve faster than surface overlap with model scale. Composite Score Breakdown: BERT’s 25% Weight Contribution Fig. 4. Composite score pie chart breakdown Fig. 4 breaks down the composite evaluation score into the fractional contribution of each metric using the weighted scheme: ROUGE-1 (0.20), ROUGE-2 (0.20), ROUGE-L (0.15), BLEU (0.10), METEOR (0.10), and BERTScore F1 (0.25). Although BERTScore F1 has the highest weight (25%), its raw values (0.83–0.87) are much larger than the n-gram scores (0.06–0.45), making it a disproportionately large contributor to the composite score. This is intentional: BERTScore captures information that n-gram metrics do not, such as paraphrasing, synonymy, and contextual relevance. The pie charts
 show that the majority of the composite score is explained by BERTScore F1 in each model, supporting its inclusion as the main discriminating measure in the evaluation pipeline. Model Ranking: Impact of BERTScore on Composite Score Fig. 5. Model ranking with/without BERTScore Fig. 5 shows the direct effect of BERTScore on the model ranking pipeline. Solid bars indicate the composite score (with BERTScore F1 weighted at 0.25) and hatched bars indicate a re-normalized composite using only n-gram based metrics (ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L, BLEU, METEOR). The addition of BERTScore raises composite scores by approximately 50–85% across all models. Importantly, the overall ranking of models is maintained — BART-CNN remains the best — proving that BERTScore does not alter the ranking but emphasizes meaningful quality differences. In lowerperforming models such as mT5-Multi, the improvement is proportionately higher, since BERTScore identifies semantic coherence even where n-gram overlap is low due to the multilingual character of the model outputs. TABLE I shows the comparison of summarization models tested on CNN/DailyMail (50000 test samples). BERTScore F1 (weight = 0.25) is a semantic quality measure that goes beyond n-gram overlap. “*” indicates the most successful model. BARTCNN scores highest on ROUGE-1 (0.445), ROUGE-2 (0.214), ROUGE-L (0.309), BLEU (0.118), METEOR (0.193), and BERTScore F1 (0.870), making it the best model under the proposed evaluation with a composite score of 0.426. The BERTScore F1 column is especially informative: even mT5Multi, which has lower n-gram scores due to its multilingual training objective, achieves a decent BERTScore F1 of 0.829, indicating that its summaries still carry semantic meaning even with low lexical overlap. The clustering of all scores within the 0.82–0.88 range indicates that all models maintain high semantic consistency and demonstrates that BERT’s contextual embeddings are sufficiently granular to distinguish quality at this scale. Metric Score Heatmap Fig. 7. Metric Score Heatmap Across All Models Fig. 7 provides a single visual overview of model performance with a normalized heatmap. The raw metric score for each cell is encoded on a Blues colormap, with a scale between 0.0 and 1.0. The contrast between the light-blue cells in the ROUGE/BLEU/METEOR section (scores 0.06– 0.45) and the deep-blue BERTScore columns (scores 0.82– 0.88) is a graphical manifestation of the key contribution that BERTScore makes to the assessment framework: it operates in a wholly different range of scores, reflecting its capability to measure semantic meaning. Row-level consistency is also visible in the heatmap, as BART-CNN and PEGASUS are the darkest rows overall, proving their superiority in both semantic and n-gram measures. The lowest row is mT5-Multi, particularly on BLEU and ROUGE-2; however, its BERTScore columns are not the lowest, proving that even a generalist multilingual model does not lose semantic integrity. VI. DISCUSSION The experimental results presented in Section ?? offer several important insights into the comparative performance of transformer-based summarization models within the COMPASS framework. Model Performance Analysis As shown in Table II, BART-large-CNN achieves the highest performance across all evaluation metrics, recording ROUGE1 of 0.445, BERTScore F1 of 0.870, and a composite score of 0.4268. This can be attributed to BART’s bidirectional encoder and autoregressive decoder architecture, which is particularly well-suited to abstractive generation tasks. PEGASUS closely follows with a composite score of 0.4215, supported by its gap-sentence generation pretraining objective, which is specifically designed for summarization tasks. The marginal difference between BART-CNN and PEGASUS (0.0053 composite score) suggests that both architectures are highly competitive on news-domain summarization. Model scale demonstrates a consistent positive effect on performance. T5-Large (composite: 0.4030) outperforms T5Base (0.3803) across all metrics, confirming that larger models capture richer contextual and semantic relationships. However, this performance gain comes with increased computational demands in terms of parameter count and inference time, representing a practical trade-off for resource-constrained deployments. BART offers a particularly favorable balance between summarization quality and computational efficiency, making it well-suited for real-world applications. mT5-multilingual records the lowest composite score (0.3490) and the weakest lexical overlap scores, as expected given its multilingual generalization objective rather than news-domain specialization. Notably however, as seen in Fig. 7, its BERTScore F1 of 0.829 remains competitive, indicating that mT5 preserves semantic coherence even where surface-level lexical overlap is reduced. This confirms that BERTScore F1 is a more reliable indicator of actual summary quality than n-gram metrics alone for multilingual models. Evaluation Framework Analysis Fig. 4, shows how BERTScore F1 has the largest contribution to our composite scoring model because of its high raw value ranges of .83-.87, compared to the low ranges of the n-gram metrics that range from 0.06-0.45. This is also intentional and justified as BERTScore captures paraphrased phrases, synonyms and relatedness in context, which all three of ROUGE, BLEU and METEOR black box approximately the same but have some exceptions. Fig. 5 illustrates that including BERTScore will not affect the order of the models (BARTCNN is still the top model), however it provides even greater quality differences between the models than the other three metrics — especially for mT5-multilingual. Limitations Several limitations of the current study should be acknowledged. First, all evaluations are conducted exclusively on the CNN/DailyMail dataset, which represents a single news domain. Generalizability of these findings to other domains such as scientific, legal, or medical text remains to be validated. Second, the dynamic model selection mechanism described in the COMPASS architecture has not been quantitatively evaluated in this study; its effectiveness relative to fixed model deployment is a direction for future work. Third, no computational benchmarks such as inference time, GPU memory usage, or parameter counts are reported, limiting the ability to make concrete efficiency comparisons across models. VII. FUTURE SCOPE The proposed summarizer system is promising in reproduceing the extractive and abstractive summaries; however,
 there are some possible enhancements to make it even more useful. Incorporating more advanced large language models (LLMs) to improve the clarity and understanding, of summaries is one possible avenue of research. Legal, medical, and other domain-specific documents can also benefit from the inclusion of domain-specific fine-tuning. A further improvement could be the use of real-time summaries of live feeds such as news feeds, meetings, and live transcripts. This could allow the system more suitable for real-time scenarios where information is constantly updated. It’s also possible to adapt the system to multimodal summarization, which involves text and other modalities such images, audio and videos. This would facilitate summarization of presentations, lectures and multimedia resources. Further enhancements may include use of better evaluation approaches, such as more advanced semantic measures and human-in-the-loop evaluation to better assess summary quality. And customisation options can be integrated to personalize summaries based on personal preferences and reading habits. At the system level, computational speed and efficiency will be crucial for real-time applications .Deployment in the cloud and integration through API can make it easier to access and use. Overall, these envisioned changes should lead to the system a smarter, more flexible and holistic summarization tool that meets the needs of different and complex real-world situations. VIII. CONCLUSION This paper proposes COMPASS (Comparative Multi- model Pipeline with Adaptive Semantic Scoring) is a multi- multimodel transformer-based text summarization system that approach that overcomes the shortcomings of the singleproaches. COMPASS brings together five abstractive transfortectures - T5-Base, T5-Large, BART-large-CNN, PEGASUSlarge, and mT5-multilingual - in one evaluation pipeline and evaluate them on CNN/DailyMail using the same experimental setup. The experimental results show that BART-large-CNN has the best performance on all metrics, recording ROUGE-1 of 0.445, BERTScore F1 of 0.870, and a composite score of 0.4268, making it the best performing under the proposed assessment methodology. PEGASUS is second with a composite score of 0.4215, thanks to ing from its summarization-specific gap-sentence pretraining. Larger model sizes perform better smaller model variants, with T5-Large (0.4030) surpassing T5-Base (0.3803). mT5-multilingual records the worst results (0.3490) due to its multilingual generalization goal instead of being news-focused, but has has a competitive BERTScore F1 (0.829), showing that the semantics is still coherent even if the words are reduced. One of the key innovations of this work is the in- velopment of a weighted aggregate scoring measure that that combines both traditional lexical (ROUGE, BLEU, METEOR) and semantic similarity (BERTScore F1), as well custom measures such as abstractiveness score and com pression ratio.This approach allows more robust, contextualmodel comparison than any individual metric, and shows that BERTScore F1 - given the highest - with a weight of 25% - is the most discriminative metric among all evaluated models. In summary, COMPASS showcases the benefits of multi-model benchmarking, token routing, and rich semantic evaluation for transformer based summarization. The framework offers a scalable and reproducible platform for future work in auization, with further prospects for domain adaptation, realtuning, real-time summarization of streaming data, and fully audio and image processing. IX. The authors would also like to acknowledge the faculty mentor for providing valuable ideas and support throughout the development of this project. Lastly, the open-source community and developers of PyTorch and HuggingFace Transformers are appreciated for making the research possible through the availability of their tools and frameworks. COMPASS: A Comparative Evaluation of Transformer-Based Abstractive Summarization Models with Composite Semantic Scoring on CNN/DailyMail Dr. A. Maheshwari Associate Professor Department of Computational Intelligence SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Kattankullathur Chennai, India maheshwa1@srmist.edu.in Abel Kurian Sangeeth Undergraduate Student Department of Computational Intelligence SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Kattankullathur Chennai, India as8259@srmist.edu.in Sanish Joseph Undergraduate Student Department of Computational Intelligence SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Kattankullathur Chennai, India sj6879@srmist.edu.in Abstract—Text summarization is an important task in the face of the steadily increasing amount of online news. This paper introduces COMPASS (Comparative Multi-model Pipeline with Adaptive Semantic Scoring), a multi-model summarization system which evaluates five transformer models, T5-Base, T5Large, BART-large-CNN, PEGASUS-large, mT5-multilingual in a single pipeline that can process inputs supporting diverse input types like text, PDFs, and URLs. We use the CNN/Daily Mail dataset to evaluate all with ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L, BLEU, METEOR and BERTScore F1, and a weighted composite of composite scoring technique that favours semantic quality over lexical overlap. Our results show that BART- large-CNN has the best results on all metrics, recording ROUGE-1 (0.445), BERTScore F1 (0.870), and a composite score of 0.4268, followed by PEGASUS (0.4215). BERTScore F1, which has the largest weight of 25% in scoring scheme, is the most discriminative scoring metric, as it measures semantic matching beyond simple level n-gram overlap. mT5-multilingual has the lowest scores due to its multilingual generalisation goal rather than newsdomain specialization. The study also demonstrates the balance between quality and efficiency across model sizes, and introduces a dynamic model selection approach that considers input length, format and language. COMPASS offers a scalable, evaluationrich platform for multi-domain automatic summarization research. Index Terms—Text Summarization, Transformer Models, T5, BART, PEGASUS, BERT, CNN/DailyMail, ROUGE. I. INTRODUCTION Text summarization is an important task in the face of the steadily increasing amount of online news. This paper introduces COMPASS (Comparative Multi-model Pipeline with Adaptive Semantic Scoring), a multi-model summariza- tion system which evaluates five transformer models - els - T5Base, T5-Large, BART-large-CNN, PEGASUS-large, mT5multilingual - in a single pipeline that can process inputs supporting diverse input types like text, PDFs, and URLs. We use the CNN/Daily Mail dataset to evaluate all with ROUGE1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L, BLEU, METEOR and BERTScore F1, and a weighted composite of composite scoring technique that favours semantic quality over lexical overlap. Our results show that BART- large-CNN has the best results on all metrics, recording ROUGE-1 (0.445), BERTScore F1 (0.870), and a composite score of 0.4268, followed by PEGASUS (0.4215). BERTScore F1, which has the largest weight of 25scoring scheme, is the most discriminative scoring metric, as it measures semantic matching beyond simple- level n-gram overlap. mT5-multilingual has the lowest scores due to its multilingual generalisation goal rather than news-domain specialization. The study also demonstrates the balance between quality and efficiency across model sizes, and introduces a dynamic model selection approach that considers input length, format and language. COMPASS offers a scalable, evaluation-rich platform for multi-domain automatic summarization research. II. LITERATURE SURVEY Early text summarization systems were mainly statistical and rule-based techniques. Extractive sum- marization was driven by techniques such as Term Frequency- Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF), sentence frequency- Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF), frequency-based sen- Rani Krishna et al. [1] give an overview of deep learning for automatic news summarization using NLP, describing the ways in which these systems analysed most important sentences from news, without important sentences of the document. Balaji and Megha [5]also showcase NLP-powered summarization rization systems based on linguistic feature extraction and statistical ranking. Although fast and simple, they were unable to produce capturing the rich contextual and semantic features in text, hence restricting the quality, smoothness and coherence of the ated summaries. Their surface lexical features meant that structurally important sentences could be
 missed when the meaning was conveyed through different words or complex syntactic constructions. The development of neural networks brought abstractive summarization using sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) mod- els using Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. Ferreira et al. [2] presented a contextual text summarizer that included discourse and context in the scoring of scoring, with enhanced context awareness compared purely statistical approaches. Dhanda and Gupta [3] also condressed this by suggesting a new machine learning-based based approach to summarization, moving away from feature engineering to learned representations of text. sentations. These neural models showed a better ability to produce human summaries. However, they had inherent problems such as vanishing graients, fixed length context windows, and severely degraded performance on longer documents. The lack of efficiency of recurrent architectures to efficiently model long range dependencies neck for sequences of arbitrary length. neck, especially in news articles and reports where key information is spread throughout the text. The game-changer in Natural Language Processing has been the advent of the Transformer model, which uses self-attention to capture long depencies over the entire input sequence at once, rather taneously rather than in a sequential manner. This allowed for pretraining on large datasets and greatly significantly boosted performance on a wide range of NLP tasks such as summarization. Gupta et al. [4] detail how to use NLP pipelines based on transformers for summarization, showing improvements in coherence and earlier recurrent approaches. Kumar et els [5]also demonstrate the success of transformer modal in different types of documents and diverse domains, confirming their potential for practical use in summarization tasks. The ability of transformers to consider all input a sequence at once, simultaneously considering local and global contextual relationships, offered a significant RNN-based systems.However, most studies in this era tested a single transformer model, providing little comparative understanding of the relative merits and trade offs of various architectures for the same summarization task. A number of transformers have since achieved state-of-theart results on summarization tasks. BART, a model with a bidirectional encoder and autoregressive decoder is especially adept at abstractive summarization of narrative and newscvlike text because of pretraining on document reconstruction tasks. PEGA- SUS, specifically pretrained for summarization with generation pretraining, has shown impressive benchmarks such as CNN/DailyMail [18]. Salaji and colleagues [7]explore doc- architectures, highlighting practical considerations in architectures, discussing challenges in practical deploy- based summarization systems in practice. Kadhim and Aghdasi [8] present an enhanced text summarization system that uses feature-based scoring and NLP techniques niques, providing a more systematic evaluation of quality assessment. But most of these systems only evaluate a single model with a single input format, and their evaluation is primarily based on lexical metrics like ROUGE and BLEU, which are known to known to penalise valid paraphrases and synonyms - a a major problem for getting at the semantic adequacy of generated summaries. Comparative studies have started to address the need for multiple models, but there is still much to be done. Muia et al. [15] compare transformer-based models for transformers for summarizing news articles, conducting different models on common datasets and discuss the dilemmas between lexical and semantic fluency in generated outputs. Bani-Almarjeh and Kurdy [9] extend the Arabic abstractive summarization from a comparative perspective with both RNN and transformer models, showing that the benefits of transformer models extend to erate to other languages and scripts. El-Kassas et al. [10]pro- give a survey of automatic text summarization methods including statistical, neural and transformer-based methods, providing a wide-ranging overview of the evolution and ongoing evaluation problems. While these compara- tive studies offer important baselines, but are confined to to lexicalbased evaluation metrics and single domain datasets, and so confine their insights to a narrow range of real-world summarisation tasks. The awareness of the need for semantic evaluation has essential supplement to lexical measures has influenced recent research directions. Adhikari [11] reviews NLP-based machine based approaches to summarisation, pointing out the in- sufficiency of n-gram overlap measures for paraphrase quality and meaning. Gambhir and Gupta [12]pro- give an overview of recent work in automatic text summarization techniques, calling for more sophisticated evaluation beyond simple word matching. Pan et al. [13] present a sequence-tosequence summarization model that that uses a topic-based attention model, and show that attention-based models can produce more topically coherent summaries. Gupta et al. [14] also explore transformer-based systems for automated news summariza- systems, highlighting the need for assessment methods that assess lexical and semantic faithfulness. The use of embedding scores like BERTScore, which measures semantic similarity based on token embeddings as a key improvement to overcome these limitations. has been a major step towards resolving these issues. Despite this, no previous work has comprehensively combined lexical and semantic metrics into a single, weighted composite assessment scheme across various transformer models, and a variety of different inputs input formats simultaneously. The current research literature, although abundant in approaches ranging from statistical methods [1], [5], neural sequence models [2], [3], and transformer-based architectures [4], [6]–[8], reveals a consistent structural gap: systems are predominantly evaluated in isolation, on single input formats, and against narrow lexical metric sets. Comparative studies [9], [10], [15] and evaluation surveys [11], [12] confirm the need for unified benchmarking frameworks that incorporate semantic assessment alongside traditional lexical measures. COMPASS addresses this divide by unifying five transformer-based abstractive models — T5-Base, T5-Large, BART-large-CNN, PEGASUS-large, and mT5-multilingual — within a single comparative pipeline, and by introducing a weighted composite scoring mechanism that integrates ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L, BLEU, METEOR, and BERTScore F1 for holistic, semantically grounded
 model evaluation across heterogeneous input formats including plain text, PDF files, and web URLs. III. DATASET DESCRIPTION The CNN/DailyMail dataset is one of the most widely used benchmarks for automatic text summarization. It consists of news articles collected from CNN and Daily Mail, each paired with human-written summaries known as ”highlights.” These highlights serve as gold-standard reference summaries for evaluating the quality of machine-generated outputs. The large scale and high annotation quality of the dataset make it well-suited for both training and benchmarking extractive and abstractive summarization models. The dataset contains approximately 287,113 training samples, 13,368 validation samples, and 11,490 test samples. Each sample consists of a full-length news article as the source text paired with a journalist-written summary comprising several sentences. The average article length is approximately 781 tokens, while the average summary length is 56 tokens. This substantial compression ratio makes the dataset particularly appropriate for evaluating the contextual understanding and information distillation capacity of summarization models. In this study, the dataset is accessed through the HuggingFace Datasets library, which provides standardized and preprocessed splits. Model-specific tokenizers corresponding to each transformer architecture — T5, BART, PEGASUS, and mT5 — are applied during preprocessing. Input sequences are truncated to a maximum of 1,024 tokens to satisfy transformer input constraints, and summary sequences are capped at 128 tokens. Padding is applied where necessary to ensure batch consistency during training. CNN/DailyMail is particularly well-suited for context-sensitive summarization tasks, as news articles are structured narratives involving multiple named entities, temporal sequences, and causal relationships. This structural richness challenges transformer-based models to capture long-range dependencies and semantic coherence across the full document. As all five models in COMPASS are evaluated on this same dataset under identical experimental conditions, it provides a reliable, consistent, and fair basis for comparative analysis. IV. PROPOSED SYSTEM / ARCHITECTURE Architecture Diagram Fig. 1. Architecture of the proposed COMPASS framework for multi-model text summarization. COMPASS is a multi-model transformer-based text summarization system designed to handle heterogeneous input formats and evaluate multiple summarization architectures under a unified framework. The system architecture is modular and consists of five core components: 1) Input Ingestion and Routing Module — Detects the format of the submitted input (plain text, PDF, or URL) and routes it to the appropriate preprocessing pipeline. 2) Dataset Management Module — Manages dataset loading, preprocessing, and split management using the HuggingFace Datasets library, with model-specific tokenization applied per architecture. 3) Model Training and Summarization Pipeline — Hosts five transformer-based abstractive models: T5-Base, T5Large, BART-large-CNN, PEGASUS-large, and mT5multilingual, each fine-tuned on CNN/DailyMail under identical hyperparameter configurations. 4) Evaluation Engine — Computes ROUGE-1, ROUGE2, ROUGE-L, BLEU, METEOR, and BERTScore F1, and aggregates them into a weighted composite score for holistic model ranking. 5) User Interface (Streamlit-based) — Provides an interactive interface for input submission, model selection, summary generation, metric visualization, and result comparison. The system workflow proceeds as follows. The user submits input through the interface, which is detected and routed by the ingestion module. The input is then preprocessed using the model-specific tokenizer, with sequences truncated to 1,024 tokens and summaries capped at 128 tokens. The preprocessed input is passed to the selected transformer model, which generates the summary. The evaluation engine then scores the output across all metrics and computes the composite rank. Final summaries and evaluation results are presented to the user through the Streamlit interface. A. Input Ingestion and Routing The system supports plain text, PDF files, and URLs as input formats. The routing module automatically detects the input type and directs it to the appropriate preprocessing pipeline. For PDF inputs, text is extracted prior to tokenization. For URLs, the article body is retrieved and cleaned before processing. Language detection is additionally performed to route non-English inputs to the mT5-multilingual model. B. Abstractive Summarization with Transformer Models The abstractive summarization pipeline incorporates five encoder-decoder transformer models: T5-Base, T5-Large, BART-large-CNN, PEGASUS-large, and mT5-multilingual. Each model is fine-tuned on the CNN/DailyMail dataset using a consistent hyperparameter configuration to ensure fair and reproducible comparison. Models are trained for 3 epochs with a batch size of 8, a learning rate of 2×10−5, and the AdamW optimizer with a linear decay scheduler. The maximum input length is set to 1,024 tokens and the maximum summary length to 128 tokens.
 C. Dynamic Model Selection COMPASS incorporates a dynamic model selection mechanism that adapts to the characteristics of the input. Input length, language, and format are used as selection signals: PEGASUS is prioritized for longer news-style documents, while mT5-multilingual is applied for non-English inputs. This selection strategy improves summarization efficiency by matching input properties to the most suitable architecture. D. Evaluation Engine COMPASS includes a comprehensive evaluation module that assesses summary quality across multiple dimensions. Standard lexical metrics — ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGEL, BLEU, and METEOR — measure n-gram overlap between generated and reference summaries. BERTScore F1 provides semantic evaluation by computing similarity using contextual token embeddings. Custom measures, including the abstractiveness score and compression ratio, assess paraphrasing capability and information density respectively. A weighted composite scoring mechanism aggregates all metrics into a single performance score using the following weights: ROUGE-1 (0.20), ROUGE-2 (0.20), ROUGEL (0.15), BLEU (0.10), METEOR (0.10), and BERTScore F1 (0.25). This composite score enables consistent, holistic ranking of all evaluated models. E. User Interface The user interface is implemented using Streamlit, providing an interactive platform for end-to-end summarization. Users can submit input in supported formats, select a summarization model, generate summaries, and view evaluation metrics. Additional features include result comparison across models, copy-to-clipboard functionality, session history tracking, and graphical visualization of metric scores. V. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS Evaluation Metrics Across All Models Fig. 2. Evaluation Metrics Across All Models Fig. 2 shows how each model performed on six evaluation metrics. The n-gram overlap measures (ROUGE-1, ROUGE2, ROUGE-L, BLEU, METEOR) produce scores between 0.06 and 0.45, which are sensitive to word-to-word matches between the generated and reference summaries. Conversely, BERTScore F1 — calculated using the contextual token embeddings of BERT — has a consistent score of 0.83–0.87 across all models. This reflects a general limitation of ngram metrics, which penalize valid paraphrases and synonyms. BERTScore balances this by assessing semantic rather than surface similarity. BART-CNN achieves the best BERTScore F1 (0.870), closely followed by PEGASUS (0.867), proving that architecturally more powerful models also generate semantically richer summaries. Radar Chart: Per-Model Metric Profile Fig. 3. Comparison of Accuracy Across Models Fig. 3 provides radar charts for each of the five models and gives a holistic view of the strength distribution across all metrics simultaneously. The BERT-F1 axis protrudes much further than the ROUGE/BLEU/METEOR axes in all models, validating that semantic quality consistently exceeds surfacelevel n-gram overlap. BART-CNN and PEGASUS demonstrate the largest and most balanced polygon areas, indicating competence across a broad range of n-gram and semantic metrics. mT5-Multi has the smallest total area, as it is trained for multilingual generalization rather than specialization on English news summarization. This visualization shows that higher-BERTScore models are also more likely to have higher n-gram scores, albeit not proportionately — semantic quality can improve faster than surface overlap with model scale. Composite Score Breakdown: BERT’s 25% Weight Contribution Fig. 4. Composite score pie chart breakdown Fig. 4 breaks down the composite evaluation score into the fractional contribution of each metric using the weighted scheme: ROUGE-1 (0.20), ROUGE-2 (0.20), ROUGE-L (0.15), BLEU (0.10), METEOR (0.10), and BERTScore F1 (0.25). Although BERTScore F1 has the highest weight (25%), its raw values (0.83–0.87) are much larger than the n-gram scores (0.06–0.45), making it a disproportionately large contributor to the composite score. This is intentional: BERTScore captures information that n-gram metrics do not, such as paraphrasing, synonymy, and contextual relevance. The pie charts
 show that the majority of the composite score is explained by BERTScore F1 in each model, supporting its inclusion as the main discriminating measure in the evaluation pipeline. Model Ranking: Impact of BERTScore on Composite Score Fig. 5. Model ranking with/without BERTScore Fig. 5 shows the direct effect of BERTScore on the model ranking pipeline. Solid bars indicate the composite score (with BERTScore F1 weighted at 0.25) and hatched bars indicate a re-normalized composite using only n-gram based metrics (ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L, BLEU, METEOR). The addition of BERTScore raises composite scores by approximately 50–85% across all models. Importantly, the overall ranking of models is maintained — BART-CNN remains the best — proving that BERTScore does not alter the ranking but emphasizes meaningful quality differences. In lowerperforming models such as mT5-Multi, the improvement is proportionately higher, since BERTScore identifies semantic coherence even where n-gram overlap is low due to the multilingual character of the model outputs. TABLE I shows the comparison of summarization models tested on CNN/DailyMail (50000 test samples). BERTScore F1 (weight = 0.25) is a semantic quality measure that goes beyond n-gram overlap. “*” indicates the most successful model. BS F1 Score BART-CNN* 0.445 0.214 0.309 0.118 0.193 0.870 0.426 Table I gives a systematic comparison of all models in terms of all metrics and the overall composite score. BARTCNN scores highest on ROUGE-1 (0.445), ROUGE-2 (0.214), ROUGE-L (0.309), BLEU (0.118), METEOR (0.193), and BERTScore F1 (0.870), making it the best model under the proposed evaluation with a composite score of 0.426. The BERTScore F1 column is especially informative: even mT5Multi, which has lower n-gram scores due to its multilingual training objective, achieves a decent BERTScore F1 of 0.829, indicating that its summaries still carry semantic meaning even with low lexical overlap. This confirms the usefulness of BERTScore as a complementary measure reflecting quality not captured by n-gram-based evaluation. The clustering of all scores in the 0.82–0.88 range indicates that all models provide semantically consistent summaries, and that BERT’s contextual embeddings are sufficiently granular to distinguish between them at this level. The raw metric score for each cell is encoded on a Blues colormap, with a scale between 0.0 and 1.0. The contrast between the light-blue cells in the ROUGE/BLEU/METEOR section (scores 0.06– 0.45) and the deep-blue BERTScore columns (scores 0.82– 0.88) is a graphical manifestation of the key contribution that BERTScore makes to the assessment framework: it operates in a wholly different range of scores, reflecting its capability to measure semantic meaning. Row-level consistency is also visible in the heatmap, as BART-CNN and PEGASUS are the darkest rows overall, proving their superiority in both semantic and n-gram measures. The lowest row is mT5-Multi, particularly on BLEU and ROUGE-2; however, its BERTScore columns are not the lowest, proving that even a generalist multilingual model does not lose semantic integrity. VI. DISCUSSION The experimental results presented in Section ?? offer several important insights into the comparative performance of transformer-based summarization models within the COMPASS framework. Model Performance Analysis As shown in Table II, BART-large-CNN achieves the highest performance across all evaluation metrics, recording ROUGE1 of 0.445, BERTScore F1 of 0.870, and a composite score of 0.4268. This can be attributed to BART’s bidirectional encoder and autoregressive decoder architecture, which is particularly well-suited to abstractive generation tasks. PEGASUS closely follows with a composite score of 0.4215, supported by its gap-sentence generation pretraining objective, which is specifically designed for summarization tasks. The marginal difference between BART-CNN and PEGASUS (0.0053 composite score) suggests that both architectures are highly competitive on news-domain summarization. Model scale demonstrates a consistent positive effect on performance. T5-Large (composite: 0.4030) outperforms T5Base (0.3803) across all metrics, confirming that larger models capture richer contextual and semantic relationships. However, this performance gain comes with increased computational demands in terms of parameter count and inference time, representing a practical trade-off for resource-constrained deployments. BART offers a particularly favorable balance between summarization quality and computational efficiency, making it well-suited for real-world applications. mT5-multilingual records the lowest composite score (0.3490) and the weakest lexical overlap scores, as expected given its multilingual generalization objective rather than news-domain specialization. Notably however, as seen in Fig. 7, its BERTScore F1 of 0.829 remains competitive, indicating that mT5 preserves semantic coherence even where surface-level lexical overlap is reduced. This confirms that BERTScore F1 is a more reliable indicator of actual summary quality than n-gram metrics alone for multilingual models. Evaluation Framework Analysis Fig. 4, shows how BERTScore F1 has the largest contribution to our composite scoring model because of its high raw value ranges of .83-.87, compared to the low ranges of the n-gram metrics that range from 0.06-0.45. This is also intentional and justified as BERTScore captures paraphrased phrases, synonyms and relatedness in context, which all three of ROUGE, BLEU and METEOR black box approximately the same but have some exceptions. Fig. 5 illustrates that including BERTScore will not affect the order of the models (BARTCNN is still the top model), however it provides even greater quality differences between the models than the other three metrics — especially for mT5-multilingual. Limitations Several limitations of the current study should be acknowledged. First, all evaluations are conducted exclusively on the CNN/DailyMail dataset, which represents a single news domain. Generalizability of these findings to other domains such as scientific, legal, or medical text remains to be validated. Second, the dynamic model selection mechanism described in the COMPASS architecture has not been quantitatively evaluated in this study; its effectiveness relative to fixed model deployment is a direction for future work. Third, no computational benchmarks such as inference time, GPU memory usage, or parameter counts are reported, limiting the ability to make concrete efficiency comparisons across models. VII. FUTURE SCOPE The proposed summarizer system is promising in reproduceing the extractive and abstractive summaries; however,
 there are some possible enhancements to make it even more useful. Incorporating more advanced large language models (LLMs) to improve the clarity and understanding, of summaries is one possible avenue of research. Legal, medical, and other domain-specific documents can also benefit from the inclusion of domain-specific fine-tuning. A further improvement could be the use of real-time summaries of live feeds such as news feeds, meetings, and live transcripts. This could allow the system more suitable for real-time scenarios where information is constantly updated. It’s also possible to adapt the system to multimodal summarization, which involves text and other modalities such images, audio and videos. This would facilitate summarization of presentations, lectures and multimedia resources. Further enhancements may include use of better evaluation approaches, such as more advanced semantic measures and human-in-the-loop evaluation to better assess summary quality. And customisation options can be integrated to personalize summaries based on personal preferences and reading habits. At the system level, computational speed and efficiency will be crucial for real-time applications .Deployment in the cloud and integration through API can make it easier to access and use. Overall, these envisioned changes should lead to the system a smarter, more flexible and holistic summarization tool that meets the needs of different and complex real-world situations. VIII. CONCLUSION This paper proposes COMPASS (Comparative Multi- model Pipeline with Adaptive Semantic Scoring) is a multi- multimodel transformer-based text summarization system that approach that overcomes the shortcomings of the singleproaches. COMPASS brings together five abstractive transfortectures - T5-Base, T5-Large, BART-large-CNN, PEGASUSlarge, and mT5-multilingual - in one evaluation pipeline and evaluate them on CNN/DailyMail using the same experimental setup. The experimental results show that BART-large-CNN has the best performance on all metrics, recording ROUGE-1 of 0.445, BERTScore F1 of 0.870, and a composite score of 0.4268, making it the best performing under the proposed assessment methodology. PEGASUS is second with a composite score of 0.4215, thanks to ing from its summarization-specific gap-sentence pretraining. Larger model sizes perform better smaller model variants, with T5-Large (0.4030) surpassing T5-Base (0.3803). mT5-multilingual records the worst results (0.3490) due to its multilingual generalization goal instead of being news-focused, but has has a competitive BERTScore F1 (0.829), showing that the semantics is still coherent even if the words are reduced. One of the key innovations of this work is the in- velopment of a weighted aggregate scoring measure that that combines both traditional lexical (ROUGE, BLEU, METEOR) and semantic similarity (BERTScore F1), as well custom measures such as abstractiveness score and com pression ratio.This approach allows more robust, contextualmodel comparison than any individual metric, and shows that BERTScore F1 - given the highest - with a weight of 25% - is the most discriminative metric among all evaluated models. In summary, COMPASS showcases the benefits of multi-model benchmarking, token routing, and rich semantic evaluation for transformer based summarization. The framework offers a scalable and reproducible platform for future work in auization, with further prospects for domain adaptation, realtuning, real-time summarization of streaming data, and fully audio and image processing. The solar system is located in the Milky Way's Orion star cluster. Only 15% of stars in the galaxy host planetary systems, and one of those stars is our own sun. Revolving around the sun are eight planets. The planets are divided into two categories, based on their composition, Terrestrial and Jovian. Terrestrial planets including Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, are primarily made of rocky material. Their surfaces are solid, they don't have ring systems, they have very few or no moons, and they are relatively small. The smallest and closest to the sun is Mercury, which has the shortest orbit in the solar system at about three Earth months. Venus is the hottest planet, with temperatures of up to 867 degrees Fahrenheit, due to an atmosphere of carbon dioxide and extensive lava flows. Next to this world of fire is a world of water, Earth. The water systems on this planet help create the only known environment in the universe capable of sustaining life. The last of the terrestrial planets, Mars, might have also supported life about 3.7 billion years ago, when the planet had a watery surface, and moist atmosphere. Beyond the four Terrestrial planets of the inner solar system lie the Jovian planets of the outer solar system. The Jovian planets include gas giants Jupiter and Saturn and ice giants Uranus and Neptune. The gas giants are predominantly made of helium and hydrogen, and the ice giants also contain rock, ice, and a liquid mixture of water, methane, and ammonia. All four Jovian planets have multiple moons, sport ring systems, have no solid surface, and are immense. The largest Jovian is also the largest planet in the solar system, Jupiter. Nearby is Saturn, the solar system's second largest planet. Its signature rings are wide enough to fit between Earth and the moon, but are barely a kilometer thick. Past Saturn are the ice giants, Uranus and Neptune. The slightly bigger of these ice giants, Uranus, is famous for rotating on its side. Next to Uranus is Neptune, the outermost planet in the solar system, and also one of the coldest. Orbiting the Terrestrial planets is the asteroid belt, a flat disc of rocky objects, full of remnants from the solar system's formation. From microscopic dust particles, to the largest known object, the dwarf planet, Ceres. Another disc of space debris lies much further out, and orbits the Jovian planets, the icy Kuiper Belt. Apart from asteroids, the Kuiper Belt is also home to dwarf planets, such as Pluto, and is the birthplace of many comets. Beyond the Kuiper Belt is the Oort Cloud, a vast, spherical collection of icy debris. It is considered the edge of the solar system since that is where the gravitational and physical influences of the sun end. Our solar system's particular configuration of planets and other celestial objects, all revolving around a life-giving star, make it a special place to call home.

COMPASS: A Comparative Evaluation of Transformer-Based Abstractive Summarization Models with Composite Semantic Scoring on CNN/DailyMail Dr. A. Maheshwari Associate Professor Department of Computational Intelligence SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Kattankullathur Chennai, India maheshwa1@srmist.edu.in Abel Kurian Sangeeth Undergraduate Student Department of Computational Intelligence SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Kattankullathur Chennai, India as8259@srmist.edu.in Sanish Joseph Undergraduate Student Department of Computational Intelligence SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Kattankullathur Chennai, India sj6879@srmist.edu.in Abstract—Text summarization is an important task in the face of the steadily increasing amount of online news. This paper introduces COMPASS (Comparative Multi-model Pipeline with Adaptive Semantic Scoring), a multi-model summarization system which evaluates five transformer models, T5-Base, T5Large, BART-large-CNN, PEGASUS-large, mT5-multilingual in a single pipeline that can process inputs supporting diverse input types like text, PDFs, and URLs. We use the CNN/Daily Mail dataset to evaluate all with ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L, BLEU, METEOR and BERTScore F1, and a weighted composite of composite scoring technique that favours semantic quality over lexical overlap. Our results show that BART- large-CNN has the best results on all metrics, recording ROUGE-1 (0.445), BERTScore F1 (0.870), and a composite score of 0.4268, followed by PEGASUS (0.4215). BERTScore F1, which has the largest weight of 25% in scoring scheme, is the most discriminative scoring metric, as it measures semantic matching beyond simple level n-gram overlap. mT5-multilingual has the lowest scores due to its multilingual generalisation goal rather than newsdomain specialization. The study also demonstrates the balance between quality and efficiency across model sizes, and introduces a dynamic model selection approach that considers input length, format and language. COMPASS offers a scalable, evaluationrich platform for multi-domain automatic summarization research. Index Terms—Text Summarization, Transformer Models, T5, BART, PEGASUS, BERT, CNN/DailyMail, ROUGE. I. INTRODUCTION Text summarization is an important task in the face of the steadily increasing amount of online news. This paper introduces COMPASS (Comparative Multi-model Pipeline with Adaptive Semantic Scoring), a multi-model summariza- tion system which evaluates five transformer models - els - T5Base, T5-Large, BART-large-CNN, PEGASUS-large, mT5multilingual - in a single pipeline that can process inputs supporting diverse input types like text, PDFs, and URLs. We use the CNN/Daily Mail dataset to evaluate all with ROUGE1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L, BLEU, METEOR and BERTScore F1, and a weighted composite of composite scoring technique that favours semantic quality over lexical overlap. Our results show that BART- large-CNN has the best results on all metrics, recording ROUGE-1 (0.445), BERTScore F1 (0.870), and a composite score of 0.4268, followed by PEGASUS (0.4215). BERTScore F1, which has the largest weight of 25scoring scheme, is the most discriminative scoring metric, as it measures semantic matching beyond simple- level n-gram overlap. mT5-multilingual has the lowest scores due to its multilingual generalisation goal rather than news-domain specialization. The study also demonstrates the balance between quality and efficiency across model sizes, and introduces a dynamic model selection approach that considers input length, format and language. COMPASS offers a scalable, evaluation-rich platform for multi-domain automatic summarization research. II. LITERATURE SURVEY Early text summarization systems were mainly statistical and rule-based techniques.
