COMPASS: A Comparative Evaluation of Transformer-Based Abstractive Summarization Models with Composite Semantic Scoring on CNN/DailyMail Dr. A. Maheshwari Associate Professor Department of Computational Intelligence SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Kattankullathur Chennai, India maheshwa1@srmist.edu.in Abel Kurian Sangeeth Undergraduate Student Department of Computational Intelligence SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Kattankullathur Chennai, India as8259@srmist.edu.in Sanish Joseph Undergraduate Student Department of Computational Intelligence SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Kattankullathur Chennai, India sj6879@srmist.edu.in Abstract—Automatic text summarization is a critical challenge in managing the growing volume of digital news content. This study presents COMPASS (Comparative Multi-model Pipeline with Adaptive Semantic Scoring), a multi-model summarization framework that benchmarks five transformer-based models — T5-Base, T5-Large, BART-large-CNN, PEGASUS-large, and mT5-multilingual — within a unified pipeline capable of handling heterogeneous input formats including text, PDFs, and URLs. All models are evaluated on the CNN/DailyMail dataset using ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L, BLEU, METEOR, and BERTScore F1, consolidated through a weighted composite scoring mechanism that prioritizes semantic quality alongside lexical overlap. Experimental results demonstrate that BARTlarge-CNN achieves the highest performance across all metrics, recording ROUGE-1 (0.445), BERTScore F1 (0.870), and a composite score of 0.4268, followed closely by PEGASUS (0.4215). BERTScore F1, assigned the highest weight of 25% in the composite scoring scheme, proves to be the most discriminating evaluation metric, capturing semantic similarity beyond surfacelevel n-gram overlap. mT5-multilingual records the lowest scores owing to its multilingual generalization objective rather than news-domain specialization. The study further highlights the trade-off between summarization quality and computational cost across model scales, and proposes a dynamic model selection strategy that adapts to input length, format, and language. COMPASS provides a scalable, evaluation-rich foundation for multi-domain automated summarization research. Index Terms—Text Summarization, Transformer Models, T5, BART, PEGASUS, BERT, CNN/DailyMail, ROUGE. I. INTRODUCTION The rapid growth of digital media, online publications, and news content platforms has led to an overwhelming flow of unstructured textual information. Manual analysis of such content is time-consuming and inefficient, particularly when users are expected to process long documents such as research papers, news articles, and reports. This growing demand has accelerated the need for intelligent automated text summarization systems capable of reducing large volumes of text into concise, contextually relevant summaries. Text summarization is one of the most important tasks in Natural Language Processing (NLP), aimed at producing shorter texts without compromising essential information. Summarization methods are broadly divided into two categories: extractive and abstractive. Extractive approaches identify and select the most relevant sentences directly from the source text, ensuring factual consistency. Abstractive approaches, in contrast, generate new sentences that semantically capture the meaning of the original content, producing more fluent and human-like summaries. Recent advances in deep learning, specifically transformerbased architectures, have substantially improved the capabilities of summarization systems. Transformers leverage selfattention mechanisms to capture long-range dependencies and contextual relationships in text, leading to improved coherence and semantic accuracy. Models such as BERT, T5, BART, and PEGASUS have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of NLP tasks, including summarization. However, most existing systems are limited to a single model or a single input format, which restricts their applicability to diverse real-world data sources. To address this limitation, this study introduces COMPASS (Comparative Multi-model Pipeline with Adaptive Semantic Scoring), a multi-model summarization framework that integrates multiple transformer architectures into a unified system. The proposed system supports heterogeneous input formats including plain text, PDF files, and web URLs, with a dynamic input routing mechanism that directs each input to the appropriate processing pipeline. The architecture is additionally designed to accommodate image and audio inputs in future extensions. Furthermore, COMPASS proposes a comprehensive evaluation framework that goes beyond classical lexical measures such as ROUGE, BLEU, and METEOR by incorporating semantic evaluation
 through BERTScore, along with custom measures including abstractiveness score and compression ratio. A weighted composite scoring mechanism aggregates these metrics to produce a holistic model performance ranking. The primary objective of this study is to develop a scalable, evaluation-rich summarization framework that enables reliable multi-model comparison, supports adaptive model selection based on input characteristics, and advances the applicability of transformerbased summarization across real-world use cases. II. LITERATURE SURVEY The earliest text summarization systems were predominantly based on statistical and rule-based methods. Extractive summarization was driven by techniques such as Term FrequencyInverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF), frequency-based sentence scoring, and graph-based methods such as TextRank. Rani Krishna et al. [1] provide a detailed overview of deep learning approaches for automated news summarization using NLP, documenting how these early systems processed large volumes of news content by identifying and extracting the most salient sentences directly from source documents. Balaji and Megha [5] similarly demonstrate NLP-based summarization pipelines grounded in linguistic feature extraction and statistical ranking. While computationally efficient and interpretable, these approaches lacked the ability to capture deep contextual associations and semantic relationships in text, thereby limiting the quality, fluency, and coherence of generated summaries. Their reliance on surface-level lexical features meant that structurally important sentences could be missed when meaning was expressed through varied vocabulary or complex syntactic constructions. The emergence of neural networks introduced abstractive summarization through sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) models based on Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architectures. Ferreira et al. [2] proposed a context-based text summarization system that incorporated discourse and situational factors into sentence scoring, demonstrating improved contextual sensitivity over purely statistical approaches. Dhanda and Gupta [3] further advanced this direction by proposing a novel machine learningdriven approach to summarization, shifting the focus from handcrafted feature engineering toward learned text representations. These neural models demonstrated an improved capacity for generating human-like summaries. However, they suffered from fundamental limitations including vanishing gradients, fixed-length context windows, and severely degraded performance on longer documents. The inability of recurrent architectures to efficiently model long-range dependencies across extended input sequences remained a persistent bottleneck, particularly for news articles and reports where critical information is often distributed across the full document. A transformative development in Natural Language Processing was the introduction of the Transformer architecture, which leverages self-attention mechanisms to model longrange dependencies across the full input sequence simultaneously, rather than processing tokens sequentially. This enabled large-scale pretraining on vast corpora and substantially improved performance across a broad range of NLP tasks including text summarization. Gupta et al. [4] detail the application of transformer-based NLP pipelines to summarization, demonstrating measurable gains in coherence and factual retention over earlier recurrent approaches. Kumar et al. [5] further validate the effectiveness of transformer models across varied document types and domains, establishing their suitability for real-world summarization applications. The capacity of transformers to attend to all positions in an input sequence simultaneously, capturing both local and global contextual relationships, represented a fundamental improvement over the sequential processing constraints of RNN-based systems. Nonetheless, the majority of studies in this period evaluated a single transformer model in isolation, offering limited comparative insight into the relative strengths and trade-offs of different architectures when applied to the same summarization task. Several transformer-based models have since demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on summarization benchmarks. BART, which combines a bidirectional encoder with an autoregressive decoder, performs particularly well on abstractive summarization of narrative and news-style texts owing to its pretraining on document reconstruction objectives. PEGASUS, purpose-built for summarization through gap-sentence generation pretraining, has demonstrated consistently strong performance on news summarization benchmarks including CNN/DailyMail [18]. Salaji and colleagues [7] explore document summarization pipelines built upon such transformer architectures, highlighting practical considerations in deploying NLP-based summarization systems at scale. Kadhim and Aghdasi [8] propose an advanced text summarization model that incorporates feature-based scoring alongside NLP techniques, offering a more structured approach to summary quality assessment. However, the majority of these systems evaluate only a single model on a single input format, and their evaluation frameworks rely predominantly on lexical overlap metrics such as ROUGE and BLEU, which are welldocumented to penalise valid paraphrases and synonyms — a significant limitation when assessing the true semantic quality of generated summaries. Comparative studies have begun to address the need for multi-model benchmarking, though important gaps persist. Muia et al. [15] conduct a comparative study of transformerbased models for news article summarization, benchmarking multiple architectures on shared datasets and highlighting trade-offs between lexical accuracy and semantic fluency in generated outputs. Bani-Almarjeh and Kurdy [9] extend the comparative perspective to Arabic abstractive summarization using both RNN-based and transformer-based architectures, demonstrating that the advantages of transformer models generalise across languages and scripts. El-Kassas et al. [10] provide a comprehensive survey of automatic text summarization techniques spanning statistical, neural, and transformer-based approaches, offering a broad view of the field’s evolution and persistent evaluation challenges. While these compara tive efforts provide valuable benchmarks, they remain largely confined to lexical evaluation frameworks and single-domain datasets, limiting the generalisability of their findings to diverse real-world summarization scenarios. The growing recognition of semantic evaluation as a necessary complement to lexical metrics has shaped more recent research directions. Adhikari [11] surveys NLP-based machine learning approaches for text summarization, noting the inadequacy of n-gram overlap metrics in capturing paraphrase quality and contextual meaning. Gambhir and Gupta [12] provide a detailed review of recent automatic text summarization techniques, advocating for richer evaluation methodologies that go beyond surface-level lexical matching. Pan et al. [13] propose a sequence-to-sequence summarization model incorporating a topic-based attention mechanism, demonstrating that attention-driven architectures can generate more topically coherent summaries. Gupta et al. [14] further investigate automated news summarization using transformer-based systems, underscoring the importance of evaluation frameworks that capture both lexical fidelity and semantic adequacy. The adoption of embedding-based measures such as BERTScore, which assesses semantic similarity using contextual token representations rather than surface n-gram overlap, has emerged as a critical advancement in addressing these evaluation gaps. Despite this awareness, no prior framework has systematically integrated both lexical and semantic metrics into a unified, weighted composite evaluation scheme applied consistently across multiple transformer architectures and heterogeneous input formats simultaneously. The existing body of literature, while rich in individual contributions spanning statistical methods [1], [5], neural sequence models [2], [3], and transformer-based architectures [4], [6]–[8], reveals a consistent structural gap: systems are predominantly evaluated in isolation, on single input formats, and against narrow lexical metric sets. Comparative studies [9], [10], [15] and evaluation surveys [11], [12] confirm the need for unified benchmarking frameworks that incorporate semantic assessment alongside traditional lexical measures. COMPASS addresses this divide by unifying five transformer-based abstractive models — T5-Base, T5-Large, BART-large-CNN, PEGASUS-large, and mT5-multilingual — within a single comparative pipeline, and by introducing a weighted composite scoring mechanism that integrates ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L, BLEU, METEOR, and BERTScore F1 for holistic, semantically grounded model evaluation across heterogeneous input formats including plain text, PDF files, and web URLs. III. DATASET DESCRIPTION The CNN/DailyMail dataset is one of the most widely used benchmarks for automatic text summarization. It consists of news articles collected from CNN and Daily Mail, each paired with human-written summaries known as ”highlights.” These highlights serve as gold-standard reference summaries for evaluating the quality of machine-generated outputs. The large scale and high annotation quality of the dataset make it well-suited for both training and benchmarking extractive and abstractive summarization models. The dataset contains approximately 287,113 training samples, 13,368 validation samples, and 11,490 test samples. Each sample consists of a full-length news article as the source text paired with a journalist-written summary comprising several sentences. The average article length is approximately 781 tokens, while the average summary length is 56 tokens. This substantial compression ratio makes the dataset particularly appropriate for evaluating the contextual understanding and information distillation capacity of summarization models. In this study, the dataset is accessed through the HuggingFace Datasets library, which provides standardized and preprocessed splits. Model-specific tokenizers corresponding to each transformer architecture — T5, BART, PEGASUS, and mT5 — are applied during preprocessing. Input sequences are truncated to a maximum of 1,024 tokens to satisfy transformer input constraints, and summary sequences are capped at 128 tokens. Padding is applied where necessary to ensure batch consistency during training. CNN/DailyMail is particularly well-suited for context-sensitive summarization tasks, as news articles are structured narratives involving multiple named entities, temporal sequences, and causal relationships. This structural richness challenges transformer-based models to capture long-range dependencies and semantic coherence across the full document. As all five models in COMPASS are evaluated on this same dataset under identical experimental conditions, it provides a reliable, consistent, and fair basis for comparative analysis. IV. PROPOSED SYSTEM / ARCHITECTURE Architecture Diagram Fig. 1. Architecture of the proposed COMPASS framework for multi-model text summarization. COMPASS is a multi-model transformer-based text summarization system designed to handle heterogeneous input formats and evaluate multiple summarization architectures under a unified framework. The system architecture is modular and consists of five core components: 1) Input Ingestion and Routing Module — Detects the format of the submitted input (plain text, PDF, or URL) and routes it to the appropriate preprocessing pipeline. 2) Dataset Management Module — Manages dataset loading, preprocessing, and split management using the HuggingFace Datasets library, with model-specific tokenization applied per architecture. 3) Model Training and Summarization Pipeline — Hosts five transformer-based abstractive models: T5-Base, T5Large, BART-large-CNN, PEGASUS-large, and mT5 multilingual, each fine-tuned on CNN/DailyMail under identical hyperparameter configurations. 4) Evaluation Engine — Computes ROUGE-1, ROUGE2, ROUGE-L, BLEU, METEOR, and BERTScore F1, and aggregates them into a weighted composite score for holistic model ranking. 5) User Interface (Streamlit-based) — Provides an interactive interface for input submission, model selection, summary generation, metric visualization, and result comparison. The system workflow proceeds as follows. The user submits input through the interface, which is detected and routed by the ingestion module. The input is then preprocessed using the model-specific tokenizer, with sequences truncated to 1,024 tokens and summaries capped at 128 tokens. The preprocessed input is passed to the selected transformer model, which generates the summary. The evaluation engine then scores the output across all metrics and computes the composite rank. Final summaries and evaluation results are presented to the user through the Streamlit interface. A. Input Ingestion and Routing The system supports plain text, PDF files, and URLs as input formats. The routing module automatically detects the input type and directs it to the appropriate preprocessing pipeline. For PDF inputs, text is extracted prior to tokenization. For URLs, the article body is retrieved and cleaned before processing. Language detection is additionally performed to route non-English inputs to the mT5-multilingual model. B. Abstractive Summarization with Transformer Models The abstractive summarization pipeline incorporates five encoder-decoder transformer models: T5-Base, T5-Large, BART-large-CNN, PEGASUS-large, and mT5-multilingual. Each model is fine-tuned on the CNN/DailyMail dataset using a consistent hyperparameter configuration to ensure fair and reproducible comparison. Models are trained for 3 epochs with a batch size of 8, a learning rate of 2×10−5, and the AdamW optimizer with a linear decay scheduler. The maximum input length is set to 1,024 tokens and the maximum summary length to 128 tokens. C. Dynamic Model Selection COMPASS incorporates a dynamic model selection mechanism that adapts to the characteristics of the input. Input length, language, and format are used as selection signals: PEGASUS is prioritized for longer news-style documents, while mT5-multilingual is applied for non-English inputs. This selection strategy improves summarization efficiency by matching input properties to the most suitable architecture. D. Evaluation Engine COMPASS includes a comprehensive evaluation module that assesses summary quality across multiple dimensions. Standard lexical metrics — ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGEL, BLEU, and METEOR — measure n-gram overlap between generated and reference summaries. BERTScore F1 provides semantic evaluation by computing similarity using contextual token embeddings. Custom measures, including the abstractiveness score and compression ratio, assess paraphrasing capability and information density respectively. A weighted composite scoring mechanism aggregates all metrics into a single performance score using the following weights: ROUGE-1 (0.20), ROUGE-2 (0.20), ROUGEL (0.15), BLEU (0.10), METEOR (0.10), and BERTScore F1 (0.25). This composite score enables consistent, holistic ranking of all evaluated models. E. User Interface The user interface is implemented using Streamlit, providing an interactive platform for end-to-end summarization. Users can submit input in supported formats, select a summarization model, generate summaries, and view evaluation metrics. Additional features include result comparison across models, copy-to-clipboard functionality, session history tracking, and graphical visualization of metric scores. V. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS Evaluation Metrics Across All Models Fig. 2. Evaluation Metrics Across All Models Fig. 2 shows how each model performed on six evaluation metrics. The n-gram overlap measures (ROUGE-1, ROUGE2, ROUGE-L, BLEU, METEOR) produce scores between 0.06 and 0.45, which are sensitive to word-to-word matches between the generated and reference summaries. Conversely, BERTScore F1 — calculated using the contextual token embeddings of BERT — has a consistent score of 0.83–0.87 across all models. This reflects a general limitation of ngram metrics, which penalize valid paraphrases and synonyms. BERTScore balances this by assessing semantic rather than surface similarity. BART-CNN achieves the best BERTScore F1 (0.870), closely followed by PEGASUS (0.867), proving that architecturally more powerful models also generate semantically richer summaries. Radar Chart: Per-Model Metric Profile Fig. 3 provides radar charts for each of the five models and gives a holistic view of the strength distribution across all metrics simultaneously. The BERT-F1 axis protrudes much further than the ROUGE/BLEU/METEOR axes in all models,

BART-CNN and PEGASUS demonstrate the largest and most balanced polygon areas, indicating competence across a broad range of n-gram and semantic metrics. mT5-Multi has the smallest total area, as it is trained for multilingual generalization rather than specialization on English news summarization. This visualization shows that higher-BERTScore models are also more likely to have higher n-gram scores, albeit not proportionately — semantic quality can improve faster than surface overlap with model scale. Composite Score Breakdown: BERT’s 25% Weight Contribution Fig. 4. Composite score pie chart breakdown Fig. 4 breaks down the composite evaluation score into the fractional contribution of each metric using the weighted scheme: ROUGE-1 (0.20), ROUGE-2 (0.20), ROUGE-L (0.15), BLEU (0.10), METEOR (0.10), and BERTScore F1 (0.25). Although BERTScore F1 has the highest weight (25%), its raw values (0.83–0.87) are much larger than the n-gram scores (0.06–0.45), making it a disproportionately large contributor to the composite score. This is intentional: BERTScore captures information that n-gram metrics do not, such as paraphrasing, synonymy, and contextual relevance. The pie charts show that the majority of the composite score is explained by BERTScore F1 in each model, supporting its inclusion as the main discriminating measure in the evaluation pipeline. Model Ranking: Impact of BERTScore on Composite Score Fig. 5 shows the direct effect of BERTScore on the model ranking pipeline. Solid bars indicate the composite score (with BERTScore F1 weighted at 0.25) and hatched bars indicate a re-normalized composite using only n-gram based metrics (ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L, BLEU, METEOR). The addition of BERTScore raises composite scores by approximately 50–85% across all models. Importantly, the overall ranking of models is maintained — BART-CNN remains the Fig. 5. Model ranking with/without BERTScore best — proving that BERTScore does not alter the ranking but emphasizes meaningful quality differences. In lowerperforming models such as mT5-Multi, the improvement is proportionately higher, since BERTScore identifies semantic coherence even where n-gram overlap is low due to the multilingual character of the model outputs. The lowest row is mT5-Multi, particularly on BLEU and ROUGE-2; however, its BERTScore columns are not the lowest, proving that even a generalist multilingual model does not lose semantic integrity. VI. DISCUSSION The experimental results presented in Section ?? offer several important insights into the comparative performance of transformer-based summarization models within the COMPASS framework. Model Performance Analysis As shown in Table II, BART-large-CNN achieves the highest performance across all evaluation metrics, recording ROUGE1 of 0.445, BERTScore F1 of 0.870, and a composite score of 0.4268. This can be attributed to BART’s bidirectional encoder and autoregressive decoder architecture, which is particularly well-suited to abstractive generation tasks. PEGASUS closely follows with a composite score of 0.4215, supported by its gap-sentence generation pretraining objective, which is specifically designed for summarization tasks. The marginal difference between BART-CNN and PEGASUS (0.0053 composite score) suggests that both architectures are highly competitive on news-domain summarization. Model scale demonstrates a consistent positive effect on performance. T5-Large (composite: 0.4030) outperforms T5Base (0.3803) across all metrics, confirming that larger models capture richer contextual and semantic relationships. However, this performance gain comes with increased computational demands in terms of parameter count and inference time, representing a practical trade-off for resource-constrained deployments. BART offers a particularly favorable balance between summarization quality and computational efficiency, making it well-suited for real-world applications.
 mT5-multilingual records the lowest composite score (0.3490) and the weakest lexical overlap scores, as expected given its multilingual generalization objective rather than news-domain specialization. Notably however, as seen in Fig. 7, its BERTScore F1 of 0.829 remains competitive, indicating that mT5 preserves semantic coherence even where surface-level lexical overlap is reduced. This confirms that BERTScore F1 is a more reliable indicator of actual summary quality than n-gram metrics alone for multilingual models. Evaluation Framework Analysis As illustrated in Fig. 4, BERTScore F1 — assigned the highest weight of 25% in the composite scoring scheme — contributes disproportionately to the composite score due to its higher raw value range (0.83–0.87) compared to n-gram metrics (0.06–0.45). This is intentional and justified: BERTScore captures paraphrasing, synonymy, and contextual relevance that ROUGE, BLEU, and METEOR systematically penalize. Importantly, as shown in Fig. 5, the inclusion of BERTScore does not alter the relative model ranking — BART-CNN remains the top-performing model — but it amplifies meaningful quality differences between models, particularly for mT5multilingual. Limitations Several limitations of the current study should be acknowledged. First, all evaluations are conducted exclusively on the CNN/DailyMail dataset, which represents a single news domain. Generalizability of these findings to other domains such as scientific, legal, or medical text remains to be validated. Second, the dynamic model selection mechanism described in the COMPASS architecture has not been quantitatively evaluated in this study; its effectiveness relative to fixed model deployment is a direction for future work. Third, no computational benchmarks such as inference time, GPU memory usage, or parameter counts are reported, limiting the ability to make concrete efficiency comparisons across models. VII. FUTURE SCOPE The suggested summarization system shows promising results in producing extractive and abstractive summaries; still, some improvements can be investigated to make it even better and more applicable in real-life settings. The addition of more sophisticated large language models (LLMs) to enhance the quality, coherence, and contextual interpretation of generated summaries is one potential direction of future work. Specialized texts like legal, medical, and technical documents can also be improved by incorporating domain-specific fine-tuning. Another possible enhancement is the adoption of real-time summarization of streaming data sources like news feeds, meetings, and live transcripts. This would make the system more appropriate for dynamic environments where information is constantly updated. It is also possible to extend the system to fully multimodal summarization, where text is combined with other inputs like images, audio, and videos. This would facilitate summarization of presentations, lectures, and multimedia materials. Additional improvements may involve the use of better evaluation methods, including more sophisticated semantic measures and human-in-the-loop evaluation to better assess summary quality. Moreover, customization features can be added to adjust summaries according to user preferences and reading habits. System-wise, optimizing computational efficiency and minimizing processing time will be essential for real-time deployment. Cloud-based deployment and API integration can also make the system more accessible and scalable. All in all, these future improvements are expected to make the system a smarter, more adaptive, and comprehensive summarization platform capable of addressing diverse and complex real-world situations. VIII. CONCLUSION This study introduces COMPASS (Comparative Multimodel Pipeline with Adaptive Semantic Scoring), a multimodel transformer-based text summarization framework that addresses the limitations of traditional single-model approaches. COMPASS unifies five abstractive transformer architectures — T5-Base, T5-Large, BART-large-CNN, PEGASUSlarge, and mT5-multilingual — within a single evaluation pipeline and benchmarks them on the CNN/DailyMail dataset under identical experimental conditions. The experimental results demonstrate that BART-large-CNN achieves the highest performance across all evaluation metrics, recording ROUGE-1 of 0.445, BERTScore F1 of 0.870, and a composite score of 0.4268, establishing it as the most effective model under the proposed evaluation framework. PEGASUS closely follows with a composite score of 0.4215, benefiting from its summarization-specific gap-sentence generation pretraining. Larger model variants consistently outperform their smaller counterparts, as evidenced by T5-Large (0.4030) surpassing T5-Base (0.3803). mT5-multilingual records the lowest scores (0.3490) owing to its multilingual generalization objective rather than news-domain specialization, though it maintains competitive BERTScore F1 (0.829), confirming that semantic coherence is preserved even where lexical overlap is reduced. One of the primary contributions of this work is the introduction of a weighted composite scoring mechanism that integrates both standard lexical metrics (ROUGE, BLEU, METEOR) and semantic evaluation via BERTScore F1, alongside custom measures including abstractiveness score and compression ratio. This framework enables more reliable, contextsensitive model comparison than any single metric alone, and demonstrates that BERTScore F1 — assigned the highest weight of 25% — is the most discriminating measure across all evaluated models. Overall, COMPASS demonstrates the effectiveness of unified multi-model benchmarking, structured input routing, and comprehensive semantic evaluation for transformer-based
 summarization. The framework provides a scalable and reproducible foundation for future research in automated summarization, with potential extensions toward domain-specific finetuning, real-time summarization of streaming data, and fully multimodal pipelines incorporating image and audio inputs. Modi was the chief minister of Gujarat from 2001 to 2014 and is the member of parliament (MP) for Varanasi. He is a member of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a right-wing Hindutva paramilitary volunteer organisation. He is the longest-serving prime minister outside the Indian National Congress.

Modi was born and raised in Vadnagar, Bombay State (present-day Gujarat), where he completed his secondary education. He was introduced to the RSS at the age of eight, becoming a full-time worker for the organisation in Gujarat in 1971. The RSS assigned him to the BJP in 1985, and he rose through the party hierarchy, becoming general secretary in 1998.[b] In 2001, Modi was appointed chief minister of Gujarat and elected to the legislative assembly soon after. His administration is considered complicit in the 2002 Gujarat violence[c] and has been criticised for its management of the crisis. According to official records, a little over 1,000 people were killed, three-quarters of whom were Muslim; independent sources estimated 2,000 deaths, mostly Muslim, with many others raped, mutilated, or both.[4] A Special Investigation Team appointed by the Supreme Court of India in 2012 found no evidence to initiate prosecution proceedings against him, causing widespread anger and disbelief among the country's Muslim communities.[d] While his policies as chief minister were credited for encouraging economic growth, his administration was criticised for failing to significantly improve health, poverty and education indices in the state.[e]

In the 2014 Indian general election, Modi led the BJP to a parliamentary majority, the first for a party since 1984. His administration increased direct foreign investment and reduced spending on healthcare, education, and social-welfare programmes. Modi began a high-profile sanitation campaign and weakened or abolished environmental and labour laws. His demonetisation of banknotes in 2016 and introduction of the Goods and Services Tax in 2017 sparked controversy. Modi's administration launched the 2019 Balakot airstrike against an alleged terrorist training camp in Pakistan; the airstrike failed,[5][6] but the action had nationalist appeal.[7] Modi's party won the 2019 general election. In its second term, his administration revoked the special status of Jammu and Kashmir and introduced the Citizenship Amendment Act, prompting widespread protests and spurring the 2020 Delhi riots in which Muslims were targeted by Hindu mobs.[8][9][10] Three controversial farm laws led to sit-ins by farmers across the country, eventually causing their formal repeal. Modi oversaw India's response to the COVID-19 pandemic, during which, according to the World Health Organization, 4.7 million Indians died.[11][12] In the 2024 general election, Modi's party lost its majority in the lower house of Parliament and formed a government leading the National Democratic Alliance coalition. Following a terrorist attack in Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir, Modi presided over the 2025 India–Pakistan conflict, which resulted in a ceasefire.

Under Modi's tenure, India has experienced democratic backsliding, or the weakening of democratic institutions, individual rights, and freedom of expression.[f][13][14] As prime minister, he has received consistently high approval ratings.[15][16][17] Modi has been described as engineering a political realignment towards right-wing politics. He remains a controversial figure domestically and internationally, over his Hindu nationalist beliefs and handling of the Gujarat riots, which have been cited as evidence of a majoritarian and exclusionary social agenda.[g]

original_text: - [Narrator] Our solar system is one of over 500 known solar systems in the entire Milky Way galaxy. The solar system came into being about 4.5 billion years ago, when a cloud of interstellar gas and dust collapsed, resulting in a solar nebula, a swirling disc of material that collided to form the solar system. The solar system is located in the Milky Way's Orion star cluster. Only 15% of stars in the galaxy host planetary systems, and one of those stars is our own sun. Revolving around the sun are eight planets. The planets are divided into two categories, based on their composition, Terrestrial and Jovian. Terrestrial planets including Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, are primarily made of rocky material. Their surfaces are solid, they don't have ring systems, they have very few or no moons, and they are relatively small. The smallest and closest to the sun is Mercury, which has the shortest orbit in the solar system at about three Earth months. Venus is the hottest planet, with temperatures of up to 867 degrees Fahrenheit, due to an atmosphere of carbon dioxide and extensive lava flows. Next to this world of fire is a world of water, Earth. The water systems on this planet help create the only known environment in the universe capable of sustaining life. The last of the terrestrial planets, Mars, might have also supported life about 3.7 billion years ago, when the planet had a watery surface, and moist atmosphere. Beyond the four Terrestrial planets of the inner solar system lie the Jovian planets of the outer solar system. The Jovian planets include gas giants Jupiter and Saturn and ice giants Uranus and Neptune. The gas giants are predominantly made of helium and hydrogen, and the ice giants also contain rock, ice, and a liquid mixture of water, methane, and ammonia. All four Jovian planets have multiple moons, sport ring systems, have no solid surface, and are immense. The largest Jovian is also the largest planet in the solar system, Jupiter. Nearby is Saturn, the solar system's second largest planet. Its signature rings are wide enough to fit between Earth and the moon, but are barely a kilometer thick. Past Saturn are the ice giants, Uranus and Neptune. The slightly bigger of these ice giants, Uranus, is famous for rotating on its side. Next to Uranus is Neptune, the outermost planet in the solar system, and also one of the coldest. Orbiting the Terrestrial planets is the asteroid belt, a flat disc of rocky objects, full of remnants from the solar system's formation. From microscopic dust particles, to the largest known object, the dwarf planet, Ceres. Another disc of space debris lies much further out, and orbits the Jovian planets, the icy Kuiper Belt. Apart from asteroids, the Kuiper Belt is also home to dwarf planets, such as Pluto, and is the birthplace of many comets. Beyond the Kuiper Belt is the Oort Cloud, a vast, spherical collection of icy debris. It is considered the edge of the solar system since that is where the gravitational and physical influences of the sun end. Our solar system's particular configuration of planets and other celestial objects, all revolving around a life-giving star, make it a special place to call home.

SRM Institute of Science and Technology is spread across six campuses — Chennai (Kattankulathur, Ramapuram, Vadapalani, Baburayanpettai), Ghaziabad and Tiruchirappalli. Those are all same off-campuses of same University with headquarters being in Chennai (Kattankulathur) as per section 3 of University Grants Commission Act, 1956. In 2017, its name was reverted to SRM Institute of Science and Technology following UGC's order to drop "University" from the name. Located about 35 km (22 mi) away from the city of Chennai, this campus is situated on a 250 acre site overlooking Grand Southern Trunk Road (GST Road), NH-32. The main campus at Kattankulathur consists of a College of Engineering and Technology, College of Medicine and Health Sciences, College of Science and Humanities, School of Management, School of Architecture and School of Law. The campus organizes events, workshops, and conferences. Vadapalani Campus is located at Vadapalani, Chennai. original_text: SRM Institute of Science and Technology (SRMIST) is a private deemed university located in Kattankulathur, (near Chennai), Tamil Nadu, India. Founded in 1985 as SRM Engineering College in Kattankulathur, it gained the deemed University status in 2002. SRM Institute of Science and Technology is spread across six campuses — Chennai (Kattankulathur, Ramapuram, Vadapalani, Baburayanpettai), Ghaziabad and Tiruchirappalli. Those are all same off-campuses of same University with headquarters being in Chennai (Kattankulathur) as per section 3 of University Grants Commission Act, 1956. It has three sister universities in Amaravati (Andhra Pradesh), Sonepet (Haryana) and Gangtok (Sikkim). SRM (Sri Ramaswamy Memorial) Engineering College, was established in 1985, followed by the other SRM colleges from 1992 to 1997. The institute gained deemed status in 2002 as SRM Institute of Science and Technology and renamed SRM University in 2006. In 2017, its name was reverted to SRM Institute of Science and Technology following UGC's order to drop "University" from the name. Located about 35 km (22 mi) away from the city of Chennai, this campus is situated on a 250 acre site overlooking Grand Southern Trunk Road (GST Road), NH-32. The main campus at Kattankulathur consists of a College of Engineering and Technology, College of Medicine and Health Sciences, College of Science and Humanities, School of Management, School of Architecture and School of Law. It is also one of the few schools in India that offers a Degree in Telecom studies. SRM Institute of Science and Technology (SRMIST), Ramapuram Campus, of the SRM Group of Institutions. Located in Chennai, Tamil Nadu, the Ramapuram campus is known for offering a wide range of undergraduate, postgraduate, and doctoral programs in fields such as engineering, management, science, and humanities. The campus is equipped with laboratories, libraries, and other facilities to support the academic and extracurricular activities of the students. The campus organizes events, workshops, and conferences. Vadapalani Campus is located at Vadapalani, Chennai. This campus houses the Faculty of Engineering and Technology, Faculty of Management, Faculty of Science and Humanities. The SRM Institute for Medical Sciences is also located within the campus. The 250-acre (100 ha) campus at Trichy on the Trichy-Chennai highway houses the faculties of Engineering & Technology, Science & Humanities, Allied Medical Science and Management. The QS World University Rankings ranked SRM Institute of Science and Technology 221st in Asia in 2025. SRM Institute of Science and Technology ranked 29th among engineering colleges in India by India Today in 2020. The National Institutional Ranking Framework (NIRF) ranked it 13th in the engineering ranking, 11th in the pharmacy ranking, 12th among universities, 24th in research and 21st overall in NIRF 2024. - Sriram Krishnan, Senior Policy Advisor of AI, White House - Nivetha Thomas, actress - Murali Vijay, cricketer - Vishnu Vishal, actor - Iswarya Menon, film actress - Neeraj Madhav, actor - Varun Chakravarthy, cricketer - Abhay Jodhpurkar, singer - Shebin Benson, actor - Vishnu Prasanna V., chess Grandmaster and coach of Gukesh D - Karthik Venkataraman, chess Grandmaster - Shrutika, Actress - Manimegalai, TV Host - "Top 20 Private Medical Universities". original_text: SRM Institute of Science and Technology (SRMIST) is a private deemed university located in Kattankulathur, (near Chennai), Tamil Nadu, India. Founded in 1985 as SRM Engineering College in Kattankulathur, it gained the deemed University status in 2002. SRM Institute of Science and Technology is spread across six campuses — Chennai (Kattankulathur, Ramapuram, Vadapalani, Baburayanpettai), Ghaziabad and Tiruchirappalli. Those are all same off-campuses of same University with headquarters being in Chennai (Kattankulathur) as per section 3 of University Grants Commission Act, 1956. It has three sister universities in Amaravati (Andhra Pradesh), Sonepet (Haryana) and Gangtok (Sikkim). SRM (Sri Ramaswamy Memorial) Engineering College, was established in 1985, followed by the other SRM colleges from 1992 to 1997. The institute gained deemed status in 2002 as SRM Institute of Science and Technology and renamed SRM University in 2006. In 2017, its name was reverted to SRM Institute of Science and Technology following UGC's order to drop "University" from the name. Located about 35 km (22 mi) away from the city of Chennai, this campus is situated on a 250 acre site overlooking Grand Southern Trunk Road (GST Road), NH-32. The main campus at Kattankulathur consists of a College of Engineering and Technology, College of Medicine and Health Sciences, College of Science and Humanities, School of Management, School of Architecture and School of Law. It is also one of the few schools in India that offers a Degree in Telecom studies. SRM Institute of Science and Technology (SRMIST), Ramapuram Campus, of the SRM Group of Institutions. Located in Chennai, Tamil Nadu, the Ramapuram campus is known for offering a wide range of undergraduate, postgraduate, and doctoral programs in fields such as engineering, management, science, and humanities. The campus is equipped with laboratories, libraries, and other facilities to support the academic and extracurricular activities of the students. The campus organizes events, workshops, and conferences. Vadapalani Campus is located at Vadapalani, Chennai. This campus houses the Faculty of Engineering and Technology, Faculty of Management, Faculty of Science and Humanities. The SRM Institute for Medical Sciences is also located within the campus. The 250-acre (100 ha) campus at Trichy on the Trichy-Chennai highway houses the faculties of Engineering & Technology, Science & Humanities, Allied Medical Science and Management. The QS World University Rankings ranked SRM Institute of Science and Technology 221st in Asia in 2025. SRM Institute of Science and Technology ranked 29th among engineering colleges in India by India Today in 2020. Price of food articles (-3.62%) decreased in January, 2025 as compared to December, 2024. The Price of crude petroleum & natural gas (6.34%), non-food articles (0.66%) and minerals (0.22%) increased in January, 2025 as compared to December, 2024. ii. Manufactured Products (Weight 64.23%): - The index for this major group increased by 0.14% to 143.2 (Provisional) in January, 2025 from 143.0 (Provisional) for the month of December, 2024. Out of the 22 NIC two-digit groups for manufactured products, 15 groups witnessed an increase in prices, 5 groups witnessed a decrease in prices and 2 groups witnessed no change in prices. Some of the important groups that showed month-over-month increase in prices were other manufacturing; manufacture of food products; machinery & equipment; chemicals & chemical products; pharmaceuticals, medicinal chemical & botanical products etc. Some of the groups that witnessed a decrease in prices were manufacture of basic metals; fabricated metal products, except machinery & equipment; wearing apparel; beverages; and other transport equipment in January, 2025 as compared to December, 2024. https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2103131&reg=3&lang=2 2/11

Antarctica isEarth'ssouthernmostandleast-populatedcontinent.Situatedalmost entirelysouthoftheAntarcticCircleandsurroundedbytheSouthernOcean(alsoknownasthe AntarcticOcean),itcontainsthegeographicSouthPole.Antarcticaisthefifth-largestcontinent,being about40%largerthanEurope,andhasanareaof14,200,000km2(5,500,000sqmi).Mostof AntarcticaiscoveredbytheAntarcticicesheet,withanaveragethicknessof1.9km(1.2mi). original_text: - [Narrator] Our solar system is one of over 500 known solar systems in the entire Milky Way galaxy. The solar system came into being about 4.5 billion years ago, when a cloud of interstellar gas and dust collapsed, resulting in a solar nebula, a swirling disc of material that collided to form the solar system. The solar system is located in the Milky Way's Orion star cluster. Only 15% of stars in the galaxy host planetary systems, and one of those stars is our own sun. Revolving around the sun are eight planets. The planets are divided into two categories, based on their composition, Terrestrial and Jovian. Terrestrial planets including Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, are primarily made of rocky material. Their surfaces are solid, they don't have ring systems, they have very few or no moons, and they are relatively small. The smallest and closest to the sun is Mercury, which has the shortest orbit in the solar system at about three Earth months. Venus is the hottest planet, with temperatures of up to 867 degrees Fahrenheit, due to an atmosphere of carbon dioxide and extensive lava flows. Next to this world of fire is a world of water, Earth. The water systems on this planet help create the only known environment in the universe capable of sustaining life. The last of the terrestrial planets, Mars, might have also supported life about 3.7 billion years ago, when the planet had a watery surface, and moist atmosphere. Beyond the four Terrestrial planets of the inner solar system lie the Jovian planets of the outer solar system. The Jovian planets include gas giants Jupiter and Saturn and ice giants Uranus and Neptune. The gas giants are predominantly made of helium and hydrogen, and the ice giants also contain rock, ice, and a liquid mixture of water, methane, and ammonia. All four Jovian planets have multiple moons, sport ring systems, have no solid surface, and are immense. The largest Jovian is also the largest planet in the solar system, Jupiter. Nearby is Saturn, the solar system's second largest planet. Its signature rings are wide enough to fit between Earth and the moon, but are barely a kilometer thick. Past Saturn are the ice giants, Uranus and Neptune. The slightly bigger of these ice giants, Uranus, is famous for rotating on its side. Next to Uranus is Neptune, the outermost planet in the solar system, and also one of the coldest. Orbiting the Terrestrial planets is the asteroid belt, a flat disc of rocky objects, full of remnants from the solar system's formation. From microscopic dust particles, to the largest known object, the dwarf planet, Ceres. Another disc of space debris lies much further out, and orbits the Jovian planets, the icy Kuiper Belt. Apart from asteroids, the Kuiper Belt is also home to dwarf planets, such as Pluto, and is the birthplace of many comets. Beyond the Kuiper Belt is the Oort Cloud, a vast, spherical collection of icy debris. It is considered the edge of the solar system since that is where the gravitational and physical influences of the sun end. Our solar system's particular configuration of planets and other celestial objects, all revolving around a life-giving star, make it a special place to call home.

www.nature.com/scientificreports OPEN Deep learning for text summarization using NLP for automated news digest K. M. Rani Krishna1, K. Somasundaram1, P. Arulmozhivarman2, Sarah A. Immanuel3 & E. R. Rajkumar4 Text Summarization, a vital aspect of natural language processing, aims to condense text while retaining its essential meaning. This process is achieved through extractive and abstractive methods. Deep Learning faces challenges in this domain, including semantic understanding, preservation of meaning, efficient handling of long documents, and ensuring coherence and grammatical correctness. Despite these challenges, deep learning offers advantages such as time saving, facilitating information retrieval, scalability, and content personalization. Also, deep learning faces the risk of losing important details, subjectivity in information selection, difficulty in handling complex texts, and variability in summary quality. Addressing these challenges remains an ongoing focus of research and development in the field of NLP. This paper proposes text summarization approach utilizing deep learning models, namely T5-base, T5-large, BART CNN, and PEGASUS. The methodology involves initial data cleaning and preprocessing of the dataset, followed by exploratory data analysis (EDA) to gain insights into the data. Subsequently, the Rouge and BLUE scores of each model are calculated to assess their summarization performance. After training the models, the Rouge and BLUE scores are re-evaluated to measure their effectiveness in generating summaries. The primary objective is to compare the performance of these models based on their Rouge scores, aiming to identify the model that provides the highest Rouge score, indicative of better summary quality. This study contributes to the advancement of text summarization techniques and provide insights into the effectiveness of various deep learning models in this domain. Keywords Text summarization, Deep learning, Abstractive text-summarization, EDA, Model evaluation, T5-base, T5-large, BART CNN-large, PEGASUS-large Considering how people are flooded with an enormous quantity of papers and information due to the internet’s exponential expansion and big data, researchers have been spurred to develop technological solutions to address this challenge. The overwhelming volume of data available online has led to a desire for automated text summarization methods to distil and condense this information into more manageable and digestible forms. Processing lengthy texts consumes significant time and resources, which may not always be feasible or practical. Text summarization A natural language processing (NLP) technique called text summarizing seeks to summarize a text while keeping its main ideas and important details. Making a condensed version of the original text that highlights the key concepts, ideas, and information is the aim of this. The task of text summary is displayed in Fig. 1. The two primary methods are below: (a) Extractive summarization Here, the summary is formed by choosing certain sentences or phrases straight from the source text. These selected sentences are typically the ones that contain the most important information, based on criteria such as relevance, importance, and frequency of occurrence. (b) Abstractive summarization This involves generating a summary that may contain new words or sentences that are absent from the source material. This method seeks to comprehend the text’s content and reword it briefly, potentially using natural language generation techniques. 1Department of Mathematics, Amrita School of Physical Science, Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Coimbatore, India. 2Center for Clean Environment, Vellore Institute of Technology, Vellore, Tamilnadu, India. 3School of Analytics and Business Information Systems, Torrens University, Adelaide, Australia. 4 Amrita School of Engineering, Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Coimbatore, India. email: s_sundaram@cb.amrita.edu; parulmozhivarman@vit.ac.in Scientific Reports | (2025) 15:36343 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-20224-1 1

Text summarization automatically generates a summary from the source document that includes all pertinent information and key phrases. In the same way that people are being overloaded with documents and information due to the internet’s exponential expansion and big data, academics are being pushed to create technical solutions to deal with this issue. The over whelming volume of data that is available online has led to a desire for automated text summaries to distil and condense this information into more manageable and digestible forms. With the proliferation of digital content, text summarization has become crucial for managing the overwhelming amount of information, particularly in the context of news articles. Modern news dissemination involves various modes, such as text, images, videos, and audio. While the textual content is essential, the context provided by accompanying media significantly enhances understanding. This complexity necessitates advanced summarization techniques that go beyond extracting key sentences to consider the broader context and multimodal inputs. Understanding a summary through human resources involves reading the text thoroughly, identifying key points and main ideas, and condensing the content into a shorter form. Figure 2 shows how humans produce summaries of a given original text document. This includes understanding the context, recognising significant details, and rewording the data in a way that makes sense and is clear. Here is how text summarization addresses these demerits: (a) Information overload management Long texts often contain redundant or irrelevant information, making it challenging for readers to identify the most pertinent points. Text summarization condenses lengthy texts into concise summaries, highlighting key information and reducing the cognitive load on readers. (b) Time efficiency Reading lengthy texts can be time-consuming, especially when users need to extract specific information quickly. Text summarization facilitates rapid information retrieval by generating succinct sumScientific Reports | (2025) 15:36343 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-20224-1 2
 www.nature.com/scientificreports/ maries that capture the main point of the text. This time-saving aspect is particularly valuable in scenarios where time is limited, such as during research or decision-making processes. (c) Resource optimisation Processing and analysing very long texts require significant computational resources and human effort. It helps optimise resource utilisation by reducing the volume of text that needs to be processed. Instead of analysing the entire document, users can focus on the summarised version, leading to more efficient resource allocation and improved productivity. (d) Enhanced accessibility Long texts can be daunting for individuals with limited time, attention span, or cognitive abilities. A summarised version can be particularly beneficial for students, professionals, and individuals with diverse learning needs, enabling them to access and understand information more effectively. In response to this, researchers have turned to technological approaches, such as NLP, machine-learning, and deep learning, to automatically summarize text. These approaches leverage computational algorithms to analyse and extract key information from textual data, generating brief synopses that highlight a document’s key elements. This work seeks to improve upon existing text summarization methods, ensuring better handling of linguistic complexities and providing more precise, contextually aware summaries. Literature review The study1 primarily focuses on Arabic abstractive text-summarization using deep learning techniques. For Arabic summarization, this study compares and utilises the performance of several model architectures, such as Transformer and RNN based models, as well as pre-trained language models like AraBERT, AraGPT2, and AraT5. Another deep learning method for abstractive text summarization in Arabic is the study by Khalil et al.2. To create logical and contextually appropriate summaries, the authors examine the difficulties and developments in producing summaries that go beyond simply extracting sentences. The project advances natural language processing (NLP) by tackling the unique linguistic challenges associated with summarising Arabic texts. The study3 discusses Automatic Text summarization (ATS) and highlights the need for it, given the explosion of internet text material. To enhance the quality of summaries, the authors proposed placing greater focus on abstractive and hybrid techniques. The work of Rahul and Monika4 provides an overview of machine learning techniques used in the NLP field for text summarization. They cover a range of techniques and their uses, giving readers a basis for comprehending machine learning’s function in textual data summarization. The importance of Automatic Text Summarization (ATS)5 is growing due to the abundance of internet content. ATS helps users efficiently retrieve important details by condensing information into brief summaries. Researchers have been working on improving summarization strategies with machine learning and optimisation techniques. This work also discusses abstractive and multilingual summarising. It goes over both intrinsic and extrinsic assessment techniques and identifies areas for future studies that improve the effectiveness of ATS. Pan et al.6 proposes a sequence-to-sequence text summarising model with a topic-based attention mechanism by emphasising topic-relevant information, this methodology improves the summary process and can provide more accurate and contextually aware summaries. This work integrates scene influence through word topic distribution to overcome a shortcoming in automatic summarization. Implicit information is not taken into consideration in traditional Seq2Seq models. Gupta et al.7 studied the automated news summarization using Transformer based pre-trained models. It addresses the need for efficient summarization due to the vast amount of online text data. Results indicate the T5 model excels, suggesting potential for future work in enhancing model robustness. Similarly, in the research paper8, Transformer-based models (GPT, T5, BART, and PEGASUS) for news article summarization are compared. In that it is discovered that T5 performs better in ROUGE metrics because of efficient fine-tuning. The importance of text summary in handling the information overload brought on by internet technology is covered in this paper9. The need for automatic text summarization in handling the growing number of scientific publications is discussed in the paper10 which compares the high accuracy of LSTM and GRU algorithms. Analyses using ROUGE indicators show that the Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) approach and its effectiveness are similar. Also, Rahman and Siddiqui11,12 proposed convolutional LSTM for abstractive text summarization. PEGASUS, a unique pre-training approach for abstractive text summarization based on extracted gapsentences, was introduced by Zhang et al.13. By filling in the blanks in a text, this method enables the model to comprehend context more fully and produce summaries that are more accurate. This research sheds light on deep learning models’ pre-training stages for summarization tasks. The use of pre-training in natural language production for text summary is covered in this study by Zhang et al.14. They investigate how pre-training can enhance generated text quality, resulting in more coherent and fluid writing. The study is important for comprehending how summarization model performance is affected by the pretraining phase. The framework proposed in15 integrates knowledge and topic extractors to improve accuracy and control. This is the conference version of the previously mentioned PEGASUS paper, in which Zhang et al.16 provides a more formal presentation of their results. The performance of the PEGASUS model and its implications for the field of NLP are discussed in detail in this publication. Yujia and Jan17 applied the reinforcement learning to abstract text summarization. Data preprocessing is a crucial step to prepare textual data for text summarization model training and evaluation. The raw text data is ready for machine learning algorithms after a few steps to clean, normalise, and arrange the data are implemented. Key steps in data preprocessing • Tokenization Breaking down text into smaller units called tokens, typically words or subworlds. The purpose of this is to convert raw text data into a structured format that models can capture and understand easily. • Normalisation Converting text data to a standard format, such as lowercase, removing punctuation, and handling special characters. • Padding and truncation Text sequences can be made to a prearranged length by truncating lengthier sequences or inserting padding characters. The main purpose is to maintain uniform input sizes for effective batch processing and training of models. • Creating attention masks Create binary masks to distinguish between padding tokens and real tokens. It helps the model disregard padding tokens during inference and training. By ignoring padding tokens, attention masks assist the model in concentrating on the pertinent portions of the input sequence. By doing this, the model’s attention processes are guaranteed to function properly, improving its ability to produce accurate summaries.  www.nature.com/scientificreports/ Models used To assess how well four cutting-edge deep learning models performed in producing acceptable and succinct summaries of a news dataset, we used them in this study. The models used in this paper are T5-base, T5-large, BART-CNN-large, and PEGASUS-large. Prior to delving into the detailed analysis of these models, we discuss the evaluation metrics used to identify the most effective model for text summarization. Specifically, we used ROUGE and BLEU scores as our primary metrics for performance assessment. These metrics and how we used them in our study are further examined in the sections below. ROUGE score ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) scores are essential for assessing how effectively the text summarization algorithm works. These metrics serve as benchmarks for the quality of summarization algorithms by objectively measuring the degree to which machine-generated summaries align with humanwritten summaries. It ranges from 0 to 1, and as the value of the rouge score is closer to 1, the model is more perfect and accurate. In the field of NLP and summarization, ROUGE scores are used to validate the efficacy of proposed methods, ensuring transparency and reproducibility of research findings. In this paper, we used three rouge score metrics as follows: 1. ROUGE-1 (Unigram Overlap) The overlap of unigrams, or single words, between the generated summary is measured by ROUGE-1. The F1-score, accuracy, and recall are computed by counting the number of overlapping unigrams. Numberof overlappingunigrams Precision = Numberof unigramsingeneratedsummary Numberof overlappingunigrams Recall= Numberof unigramsinreferencesummary 2. ROUGE-2 (bigram overlap) The overlap of bigrams, or pairs of adjacent words, between the reference summary and the generated summary is measured using ROUGE-2. It broadens the assessment to include additional semantic data. 3. ROUGE-L (longest common subsequence) The longest common subsequence (LCS) between the reference summary and the generated summary is measured by ROUGE-L. Instead of concentrating on word overlap, it considers the longest word sequence that appears in both summaries. By evaluating the degree to which generated summaries match the summaries authored by humans, ROUGE scores shed insight into the quality of these summaries. Better summarising performance is demonstrated by higher ROUGE scores, and every measure presents a unique angle on the summarization procedure. ROUGE-2 builds on ROUGE-1’s surface-level lexical overlap recognition to include bigrams and more contextual information. When analysing the longest common sequence, ROUGE-L places a strong emphasis on content overlap, which is essential for accurately summarising the original text. All things considered, these requirements are essential for directing the creation and assessment of text summarising systems since they offer an objective assessment of summary quality. Bleu score Text summarization and machine translation systems are evaluated on their text quality using standards called BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) scores. They evaluate the degree to which the generated text is comparable to reference texts, which are usually summaries or translations provided by humans. Although BLEU is more frequently linked to machine translation, text summarization also makes use of it. The scores range from 0 to 1, where 1 indicates a perfect match between the generated summary and the reference summary. However, achieving a score close to 1 is very rare. Role in Text Summarization: • Precision-based metric When contrasting the reference summaries with the generated summary, BLEU analyses the accuracy of n-grammes, or sequences of n-words. This indicates that the number of n-grammes in the generated text matches those in the reference text. • Multi-ngram analysis BLEU preserves both surface-level vocabulary matches and more complex contextual matches by considering unigrams, bigrams, trigrams, and higher-order n-grams. This offers an accurate assessment of the substance and flow of the summary. BLEU scores offer an accepted technique for comparing and enhancing the field by offering a standard for evaluating the efficacy of various summarization methods. Google Research created T5, which standardises Scientific Reports | (2025) 15:36343 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-20224-1 7

Modelling hidden text lengths enhances contextual and semantic understanding during pre-training. The models’ ability to produce clear and coherent summaries are optimised through post-training fine tuning on certain summarising datasets. The role of it in text summarization lies in handling long inputs, generating summaries, customization and versatility. By recognising connections and relationships within the text, the transformer architecture of T5-base effectively handles extended text sequences, which are essential for summarising jobs. It is also able to generate summaries that accurately capture the major ideas of the original text due to its encoder-decoder architecture, which has been improved by intensive pre-training. It is also flexible enough to be used in a variety of areas and can be adapted to meet varied summarization demands, such as summarising studies on news items. With its dominant transformer-based development and unified approach, it is essential for text summarization. It is an important tool in NLP given its capacity to handle lengthy texts, produce logical results, and adjust to various jobs. The initial test performed when testing the dataset using the T5 base model produced a moderate initial result, with an average ROUGE score of approximately 0.29 and a BLEU score of 0.0431. Table 3 shows the average scores during testing the dataset. The score shows a considerable improvement following the model’s fine-tuning using a task-specific dataset. Also, this improvement shows how fine-tuning makes a difference in helping the model accurately capture and recreate important aspects of the source text in its summaries. The outcome shows how well the T5 base model can summarise text, particularly when adjusted to the unique features of the dataset, which produces summaries that are more precise and logical. T5-LARGE A member of the transformer family, the T5 large model was developed by Google Research. Every NLP task is considered by the T5 architecture as a text-to-text task, implying that text strings are consistently utilised for both the input and output. This method provides the use of a single framework for a variety of tasks, including text summarization, question answering, and translation. In comparison with smaller models, the T5 large is superior and capable of handling complex language interpretation and creation tasks since it has 24 layers and 770 million parameters. Using an elimination auto-encoding objective, the model is pre-trained on a large corpus of different text data, where it gains the ability to detect missing tokens in a distorted input sequence. This extensive pre-training helps in T5’s development of strong linguistic knowledge. Its role of it in text summarization, it excels at text summarising, generating clear, understandable summaries of lengthy texts. It is capable of capturing complex connections and interpretations inside the text because of its immense parameter count and thorough pre-training. Since it enables the model to autonomously handle the task as a sequence-to-sequence problem, the content-to-text framework is highly beneficial for summary. It converts an input document (source text) into a brief version (summary), preserving important context and information. To use T5-large for summarization, the pre-trained model needs to be modified using a specific summarization dataset. In the process of fine-tuning, the model develops the capacity to provide summaries that are relevant to the style and requirements of the dataset. T5-large’s strong language processing abilities ensure that the summaries generated are not only grammatically and naturally correct but also informative. It is a useful tool for managing the massive quantity of textual information encountered in modern applications since it can provide high-quality, coherent, and short summaries by utilising its extensive pre-training and smart architecture. The model structure of T5 is shown in Fig. 5. In the initial testing of the dataset using T5-large, the output average ROUGE score was approximately 0.2429 and the BLEU score was 0.0338. Table 4 shows the average rouge and bleu scores of testing the dataset. As we see, compared to T5-large, T5-base has a higher score. BART-LARGE-CNN Facebook AI developed the transformer-based BART (Bidirectional and Auto-Regressive Transformers) model specifically for sequence-to-sequence tasks like text summarization. A modified version of the BART model known as the “large CNN” variant includes a huge architecture with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) integrated into its layers. The benefits of auto-regressive and bidirectional transformers merge in BART. It consists of a left-to-right auto-regressive decoder, like GPT, that generates output text one token at a time, and a bidirectional encoder, like BERT, that scans the full input text to grasp context. Because of its dual nature, BART can handle jobs that call for producing coherent and contextually relevant text (output sequence) as well as understanding context (input sequence). In the process, BART-large CNN plays an important role by transforming lengthy and complex text into a shorter summary while retaining the original meaning and key information. PEGASUS-large The most advanced model built specifically for text summarising tasks is called PEGASUS (Pre-training with Extracted Gap-Sentences for Abstractive Summarising Sequence-to-Sequence). PEGASUS is a highly efficient method for producing high-quality summaries because it uses a new pre-training objective developed for summary, which was created by researchers at Google Research. The Transformer architecture, a deep learning model built for NLP tasks, constitutes basis for PEGASUS. The encoder-decoder structure of PEGASUS is similar to that of other Transformer models. The input text is analysed by the encoder, and the summary has been generated by the decoder. PEGASUS’s pre-training methodology is its main innovation. It includes a novel technique known as “GapSentence Generation (GSG),” in contrast to traditional models that have already been pre-trained with generic language modelling tasks. The key terms in GSG are masked off, and the model learns how to recognise these gaps from the rest of the text. CNN/daily-mail news The CNN/Daily-Mail dataset is sourced directly from the Hugging Face ‘datasets’ library20. A well-known resource for building and evaluating text summarising models is the CNN/Daily Mail dataset. Since its initial introduction in 2015 by Karl Moritz Hermann and associates, it has established itself as a standard for evaluating summarization algorithms’ performance. This dataset is perfect for extractive and abstractive summarization models because it includes summaries of news stories from CNN and the Daily Mail. The dataset contains over 300,000 unique news articles. Results and discussions Using the CNN/Daily Mail dataset, this study attempts to assess how well different deep learning models perform on the text summarising task. The technique comprises multiple pivotal steps: gathering data, preparing data, training and testing models, and assessing performance. T5 base, T5 large, BART CNN large, and PEGASUS large are the models that are assessed in this investigation. As we discussed already, the paper involves these steps: Data collection: This study uses the CNN/Daily-Mail dataset. The news documents in this dataset, along with the summaries that go with them, are suitable for training and testing text summarization models. Data preparation: Reduces unnecessary characters, HTML tags, and non-text elements to ensure consistency and quality. To ensure stable sequence lengths, text is tokenized into sub- word units, padded, and shortened. In order to help the model stay focused during training, attention masks have been created to distinguish between real tokens and padding. Model-Training: In this study, the model-training process involves multiple organised phases, each of which improves the models’ ability for summarization. Below is an overview of the methods that were used: • Setting training parameters To effectively direct the training process, key hyperparameters like learning rate, batch size, epochs, and methods for optimisation are carefully set. Based on accepted best practices for deep learning model training, these parameters were chosen. • Training the models The models are successively trained to reduce the loss function using gradient descent and backpropagation. Through this procedure, the models can improve their capacity to produce precise summaries by gaining insight from the subtleties of the CNN/Daily-Mail dataset. • Validation To assess how well the models performed and avoid overfitting, they are frequently assessed on the validation set. To make sure the models generate clear summaries and are well-generalised, this required analysing a variety of metrics. • Iterative optimisation Continuous improvements are made to the training procedure based on validation outcomes. The models can gradually enhance their summarising skills because of this iterative process. • Generalisation The models’ strong performance in summarising news items from the dataset is ensured by their rigorous training and validation, which showed that they could generalise well to previously unseen material. Our four models are effectively taught to produce precise and perceptive summaries by closely adhering to this extensive training process, which offered insightful information about the news items’ content from the dataset. Primarily, it focuses on assessing the CNN-DailyMail dataset, a benchmark in the field of NLP, to assess the performance of four deep learning models: T5-base, T5-large, BART CNN-large, and PEGASUS-large. The quality of the summaries produced by these models are evaluated using evaluation metrics such as rouge and bleu scores. The study emphasises how crucial text summaries are for controlling information overload, making the most use of available resources, and improving information accessibility. The findings indicate that the BART CNN model outperforms the other models in terms of ROUGE and BLEU scores, suggesting it is the most effective for generating high-quality summaries from the dataset. This model’s superior performance can be attributed to its sophisticated architecture and extensive pre-training, which enable it to produce coherent and contextually accurate summaries. The paper contributes to the advancement of text summarization techniques and provides valuable insights into the comparative performance of various deep learning models. Also, the methodological approach, which includes data cleaning, preprocessing, and rigorous model training and validation, ensures the reliability of the results. In conclusion, the study demonstrates the potential of deep learning models, particularly the BART CNN model, in automating the summarization of textual content. The research underscores the ongoing efforts in the field of NLP to develop more efficient and accurate text summarization methods that can handle the complexities of natural language and provide precise, contextually aware summaries.
